Sports Minister [M. S. Gill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._S._Gill "M. S. Gill") meeting with the athletes at the [Games Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_Village "2010 Commonwealth Games Village")

The [New Delhi Municipal Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi_Municipal_Council "New Delhi Municipal Council") building served as the headquarters of the Commonwealth Games Organizing Committee.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Venue-8) The [Commonwealth Games Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_Village "2010 Commonwealth Games Village") provided accommodation and training for athletes of the Games. It was spread over an area of 63.5 ha (157 acres), along the east bank of the [Yamuna River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamuna_River "Yamuna River"). It consisted of five zones—the Residential Zone, the International Zone, the Training Area, the Main Dining, and the Operational Zone, and was accessible to [para-sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disabled_sports "Disabled sports") athletes as well.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-12) Athletes and accompanying delegates were provided free food and accommodation at the Games Village.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-List-13)

### Budget

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Budget")]

The initial budget for hosting the Games as estimated by the [Indian Olympic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Olympic_Association "Indian Olympic Association") (IOA) in 2003 was ₹16.2 billion (US$170 million). However, the total budget escalated to an estimated ₹115 billion (US$1.2 billion), which excluded non-sports-related infrastructure development.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-14) The overall cost of hosting the Games was estimated to be ₹700 billion (US$7.3 billion),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-15) making it the most expensive Commonwealth Games ever.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-16)

### Infrastructure and facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Infrastructure and facilities")]

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/f/f1/CWGGreenGamesLogo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CWGGreenGamesLogo.jpg)

Logo of the "Green Games" initiative

The organisers signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the [United Nations Environment Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Environment_Programme "United Nations Environment Programme") to launch the "Green Games" initiative, aimed at adopting environmentally sustainable practices and reducing the [carbon footprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint") during the Games.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-17)

A four-lane, 5 km (3.1 mi)-long elevated road, from [Lodhi Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lodhi_Road "Lodhi Road") to [Sarai Kale Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarai_Kale_Khan "Sarai Kale Khan"), linking the Games Village to the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, was constructed, to reduce the travel time between the venues from the usual 40 minutes to six minutes. The [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") spent over ₹160 billion (US$1.7 billion) for upgrading public infrastructure in Delhi. This included the construction of new bridges, flyovers, and underpasses, widening and relaying arterial roads, installation of new traffic signs and bus shelters, and beautifying public areas.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-HT-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-TOI-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Rediff-20) Dedicated lanes were introduced on selected highways to facilitate faster movement between the sporting venues and the Games village.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-List-13)

Over 3,500 new low-floor buses were introduced by the [Delhi Transport Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Transport_Corporation "Delhi Transport Corporation") to cater to the transport requirements of the athletes and spectators.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-HT-18)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Rediff-20) Athletes and delegated were provided free transport to and from the sporting venues, and a free sightseeing trip to the [Taj Mahal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal "Taj Mahal").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-List-13) The [Delhi Tourism and Transportation Development Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Tourism_and_Transportation_Development_Corporation "Delhi Tourism and Transportation Development Corporation") launched India's first [Hop-On Hop-Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hop-On_Hop-Off "Hop-On Hop-Off") bus service (HOHO Delhi), which were equipped with digital video screens, and trained guides for providing information to the tourists.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-21)[Radio Frequency Identification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Frequency_Identification "Radio Frequency Identification") was used to tag vehicles in parking lots at the sporting venues to help organise mass parking and increase security.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-22)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Delhi2.jpg/250px-Delhi2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Delhi2.jpg)

The second phase of the [Delhi Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Metro "Delhi Metro") was completed ahead of the Games

The [Delhi Metro Rail Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Metro_Rail_Corporation "Delhi Metro Rail Corporation") completed the second phase of the [Delhi Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Metro "Delhi Metro"), extending to 125 km (78 mi), ahead of the Commonwealth Games.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-24) The [Indira Gandhi International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi_International_Airport "Indira Gandhi International Airport") was modernised, and expanded. A [new terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi_International_Airport#Terminal_3 "Indira Gandhi International Airport"), spread over 500,000 ft 2 (46,000 m 2), was constructed at a cost of $2 billion, and was capable of handling 34 million passengers per annum.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-25) A third runway had been added in 2008, which enabled the airport to operate more than 70 flights an hour.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-26)

In preparation for the expected influx of [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language")-speaking tourists for the Games, the [Government of Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Delhi "Government of Delhi") implemented a program to teach English for cab drivers, [security workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_guard "Security guard"), waiters, porters, and other service staff.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-27) To cater to the power requirements, the government increased the power generation capacity, and upgraded the power infrastructure and power distribution networks.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-28) A large-scale construction and beautification project was undertaken, that resulted in the demolition of hundreds of temporary homes and shelters.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Slum-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-30) Bamboo screens were erected around city's slums to hide them from the sights of the visitors.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-31) Beggars were relocated from the city's streets, and the [Delhi High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_High_Court "Delhi High Court") set up mobile courts that determined whether each beggar was to be sent back to his/her state of residence, or be permitted to remain in government-shelters.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-33)

### Queen's baton relay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Queen's baton relay")]

The [Queen's Baton Relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Baton_Relay "Queen's Baton Relay") was inaugurated at the [Buckingham Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace "Buckingham Palace") on 29 October 2009. The baton, containing a message from [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") to the athletes, visited 69 Commonwealth nations before reaching India.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-34) It arrived in India on 25 June 2010 through the [Wagah Border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagah_Border "Wagah Border") crossing from Pakistan.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-35) The baton was designed by Foley Design studio and was created by [Titan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_Company "Titan Company") in collaboration with [Bharat Electronics Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharat_Electronics_Limited "Bharat Electronics Limited"). The 664 mm (26.1 in)-high baton weighed 1.9 kg (4.2 lb), and consisted of a triangular section of [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium") twisted into a [helix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helix "Helix") shape and then coated with soils collected from various regions of India. A jewel-encrusted box was used to house the Queen's message, which was laser-engraved onto a 18 carat [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") leaf. The baton was illuminated by several [LEDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED "LED"), capable of producing various illuminated designs.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-36)

### Opening ceremony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Opening ceremony")]

Main article: [2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/A_spectacular_view_of_Jawahar_Lal_Nehru_stadium_during_the_opening_ceremony_of_the_19th_Commonwealth_Games_2010-Delhi%2C_in_New_Delhi_on_October_03%2C_2010_%281%29.jpg/250px-A_spectacular_view_of_Jawahar_Lal_Nehru_stadium_during_the_opening_ceremony_of_the_19th_Commonwealth_Games_2010-Delhi%2C_in_New_Delhi_on_October_03%2C_2010_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_spectacular_view_of_Jawahar_Lal_Nehru_stadium_during_the_opening_ceremony_of_the_19th_Commonwealth_Games_2010-Delhi,_in_New_Delhi_on_October_03,_2010_(1).jpg)

[Opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony") at the [Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru_Stadium_(Delhi) "Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium (Delhi)")

The opening ceremony was held at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, the main stadium of the event. It began at 19:00[IST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Standard_Time "Indian Standard Time") on 3 October.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-37) The opening ceremony was directed by [Bharat Bala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharat_Bala "Bharat Bala"). It featured over 8,000 performers, and lasted for two-and-a-half hours.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-38) It was estimated to have costed ₹3.5 billion (equivalent to ₹7.9 billion or US$82 million in 2023).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-39)

The ceremony was divided into six separate segments, each showcasing the diverse cultures of India. The countdown took place on the large screen in the stadium, and was accompanied by [fireworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireworks "Fireworks"). The centerpiece of the ceremony was the helium [aerostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerostat "Aerostat"), which acted as a giant 360° screen for spectators. It began with a showcase of a variety of [drummers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummer "Drummer") from all parts of India, accompanied by seven-year-old [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla") player. The ceremony showcased a fusion of various classical dances from all parts of India, [mehendi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehendi "Mehendi") decorations, sand paintings, and [yoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoga "Yoga"). The title song was performed by [A. R. Rahman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._R._Rahman "A. R. Rahman"), and singer [Hariharan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hariharan_(singer) "Hariharan (singer)") sang the welcome song for the Games, titled "Swagatam", along with thousands of school children.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-40)

[Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III "Charles III"), the [Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales "Prince of Wales") (representing Elizabeth II as the [Head of the Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_the_Commonwealth "Head of the Commonwealth")) and [Pratibha Patil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratibha_Patil "Pratibha Patil"), the [President of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_India "President of India"), officially declared the Games open.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-41)[Manmohan Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manmohan_Singh "Manmohan Singh"), the [Prime Minister of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India"), and three [heads of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heads_of_state "Heads of state")–[Mohamed Nasheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Nasheed "Mohamed Nasheed"), the [President of the Maldives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Maldives "President of the Maldives"), [Marcus Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Stephen "Marcus Stephen"), the [President of Nauru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Nauru "President of Nauru"), [Albert II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_II,_Prince_of_Monaco "Albert II, Prince of Monaco"), the [Prince of Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Monaco "Prince of Monaco"), and [Anand Satyanand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anand_Satyanand "Anand Satyanand"), the [Governor General of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General_of_New_Zealand "Governor General of New Zealand"), attended the ceremony.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-43)

### Closing ceremony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Closing ceremony")]

Main article: [2010 Commonwealth Games closing ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_closing_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games closing ceremony")

The closing ceremony was held on 14 October 2014 at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-44) and featured Indian and Scottish performers.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-46) The Commonwealth Games flag was handed over to representatives of [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"), Scotland, which was to host the [XX Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Commonwealth_Games "2014 Commonwealth Games") in 2014.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-47)

[Kabaddi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaddi "Kabaddi") was a demonstration sport at the Games.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-118)[Triathlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triathlon "Triathlon") was excluded from the Games as there was no suitable location to conduct the swimming stage of the competition.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-119)[Basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") was excluded, while [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"), [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis"), and [wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestling "Wrestling"), which were not contested in the 2006 Commonwealth Games, made a comeback.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-120) Despite popular demand, [Cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket") was not included, as the [Board of Control for Cricket in India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Control_for_Cricket_in_India "Board of Control for Cricket in India") were not keen on a [Twenty20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty20 "Twenty20") tournament, and the Games organisers did not want a [one day tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_day_tournament "One day tournament").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-121)

The **2010 Commonwealth Games**, officially known as the **XIX Commonwealth Games** and commonly known as **Delhi 2010**, was an international [multi-sport event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-sport_event "Multi-sport event") for the members of the [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") that was held in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), India, from 3 to 14 October 2010.

A total of 4,352 athletes from 71 Commonwealth nations and dependencies competed 272 events across 21 sports making it the largest [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games "Commonwealth Games"), in terms of participation, to date. It was the largest international multi-sport event staged in India, which had previously hosted the [Asian Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Games "Asian Games") in [1951](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1951_Asian_Games "1951 Asian Games") and [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Asian_Games "1982 Asian Games"). It was the first time that the Commonwealth Games were held in India and the second time it was held in Asia after [Kuala Lumpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuala_Lumpur "Kuala Lumpur") in [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Commonwealth_Games "1998 Commonwealth Games").

The events were held across [12 venues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venues_of_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Venues of the 2010 Commonwealth Games"). The [opening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony") and [closing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_closing_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games closing ceremony") ceremonies were held at the [Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru_Stadium,_Delhi "Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, Delhi"), the main venue of the event. The preparation for the Games received widespread media attention, with [criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concerns_and_controversies_over_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Concerns and controversies over the 2010 Commonwealth Games") directed at the organisers for the slow pace of progress in the work related to the Games, and issues related to security and hygiene. However, the works were completed in time for the Games, and it went ahead as per schedule.

While some nations threatened with boycotts, all members of the Commonwealth participated in the event, with the exception of [Fiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji "Fiji"), which was [suspended from the Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suspension_from_the_Commonwealth_of_Nations "Suspension from the Commonwealth of Nations"), and [Tokelau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokelau "Tokelau"), which didn't send a team. [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Australia at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") led the [medal tally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table "2010 Commonwealth Games medal table") with 177 medals including 74 golds. The host nation, India, achieved its best performance ever at the [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_at_the_Commonwealth_Games "India at the Commonwealth Games"), finishing second, winning 101 medals including 38 golds.

## Host selection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Host selection")]

The host city of the 2010 Commonwealth Games was selected on 14 November 2003 during the [Commonwealth Games Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_Federation "Commonwealth Games Federation") (CGF) General Assembly in [Montego Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montego_Bay "Montego Bay"), Jamaica. Delhi, India competed with [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Ontario "Hamilton, Ontario"), Canada, for the rights to host the Games.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-2) India's bid was under the motto _New Frontiers and Friendships_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-3) India committed to give US$100,000 to each of the participating associations to train athletes, for a total of $7.2 million, while Canada offered $3.8 million.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Host-4) Delhi had earlier bid for the [1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Commonwealth_Games "1990 Commonwealth Games") and [1994 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Commonwealth_Games "1994 Commonwealth Games") but lost to [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland") and [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_British_Columbia "Victoria, British Columbia") respectively. The Hamilton bid was Canada's attempt to hold the games for the fifth time.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-6) While Delhi had not previously hosted the Commonwealth Games, [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") was awarded the hosting rights of the [2010 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Winter_Olympics "2010 Winter Olympics") earlier in the year, and observers opined that the Olympics might upstage the Commonwealth Games.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-7) Delhi won the hosting rights over Hamilton with a 46-22 vote.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Host-4)

The [Indira Gandhi Sports Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi_Arena "Indira Gandhi Arena"), and [Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru_Stadium,_New_Delhi "Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, New Delhi") underwent major renovations or an uplift. The largest venue was the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, with a capacity of 60,000, was the main venue of the event, hosting both the [opening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony") and the [closing ceremonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_closing_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games closing ceremony").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-9)

Twenty training venues were used for the Games, of which one was used for [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"); three for [aquatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquatics "Aquatics"); two for [lawn bowls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_bowls "Lawn bowls"); two for [netball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netball "Netball"); eight for [rugby sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_sevens "Rugby sevens"); two for [shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_shooting "Sports shooting"); one for [squash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squash_(sport) "Squash (sport)"); two for [table tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_tennis "Table tennis"); one for [weightlifting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_weightlifting "Olympic weightlifting"), three for [wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestling "Wrestling"), and two for [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-10)

### Budget

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Budget")]

The initial budget for hosting the Games as estimated by the [Indian Olympic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Olympic_Association "Indian Olympic Association") (IOA) in 2003 was ₹16.2 billion (US$170 million). However, the total budget escalated to an estimated ₹115 billion (US$1.2 billion), which excluded non-sports-related infrastructure development.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-14) The overall cost of hosting the Games was estimated to be ₹700 billion (US$7.3 billion),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-15) making it the most expensive Commonwealth Games ever.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-16)

### Infrastructure and facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Infrastructure and facilities")]

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/f/f1/CWGGreenGamesLogo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CWGGreenGamesLogo.jpg)

Logo of the "Green Games" initiative

The organisers signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the [United Nations Environment Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Environment_Programme "United Nations Environment Programme") to launch the "Green Games" initiative, aimed at adopting environmentally sustainable practices and reducing the [carbon footprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint") during the Games.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-17)

A four-lane, 5 km (3.1 mi)-long elevated road, from [Lodhi Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lodhi_Road "Lodhi Road") to [Sarai Kale Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarai_Kale_Khan "Sarai Kale Khan"), linking the Games Village to the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, was constructed, to reduce the travel time between the venues from the usual 40 minutes to six minutes. The [Government of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") spent over ₹160 billion (US$1.7 billion) for upgrading public infrastructure in Delhi. This included the construction of new bridges, flyovers, and underpasses, widening and relaying arterial roads, installation of new traffic signs and bus shelters, and beautifying public areas.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-HT-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-TOI-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Rediff-20) Dedicated lanes were introduced on selected highways to facilitate faster movement between the sporting venues and the Games village.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-List-13)

Over 3,500 new low-floor buses were introduced by the [Delhi Transport Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Transport_Corporation "Delhi Transport Corporation") to cater to the transport requirements of the athletes and spectators.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-HT-18)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Rediff-20) Athletes and delegated were provided free transport to and from the sporting venues, and a free sightseeing trip to the [Taj Mahal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taj_Mahal "Taj Mahal").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-List-13) The [Delhi Tourism and Transportation Development Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Tourism_and_Transportation_Development_Corporation "Delhi Tourism and Transportation Development Corporation") launched India's first [Hop-On Hop-Off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hop-On_Hop-Off "Hop-On Hop-Off") bus service (HOHO Delhi), which were equipped with digital video screens, and trained guides for providing information to the tourists.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-21)[Radio Frequency Identification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Frequency_Identification "Radio Frequency Identification") was used to tag vehicles in parking lots at the sporting venues to help organise mass parking and increase security.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-22)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Delhi2.jpg/250px-Delhi2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Delhi2.jpg)

The second phase of the [Delhi Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Metro "Delhi Metro") was completed ahead of the Games

The [Delhi Metro Rail Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Metro_Rail_Corporation "Delhi Metro Rail Corporation") completed the second phase of the [Delhi Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Metro "Delhi Metro"), extending to 125 km (78 mi), ahead of the Commonwealth Games.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-24) The [Indira Gandhi International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi_International_Airport "Indira Gandhi International Airport") was modernised, and expanded. A [new terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi_International_Airport#Terminal_3 "Indira Gandhi International Airport"), spread over 500,000 ft 2 (46,000 m 2), was constructed at a cost of $2 billion, and was capable of handling 34 million passengers per annum.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-25) A third runway had been added in 2008, which enabled the airport to operate more than 70 flights an hour.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-26)

In preparation for the expected influx of [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language")-speaking tourists for the Games, the [Government of Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Delhi "Government of Delhi") implemented a program to teach English for cab drivers, [security workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Security_guard "Security guard"), waiters, porters, and other service staff.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-27) To cater to the power requirements, the government increased the power generation capacity, and upgraded the power infrastructure and power distribution networks.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-28) A large-scale construction and beautification project was undertaken, that resulted in the demolition of hundreds of temporary homes and shelters.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Slum-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-30) Bamboo screens were erected around city's slums to hide them from the sights of the visitors.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-31) Beggars were relocated from the city's streets, and the [Delhi High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_High_Court "Delhi High Court") set up mobile courts that determined whether each beggar was to be sent back to his/her state of residence, or be permitted to remain in government-shelters.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-33)

### Queen's baton relay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Queen's baton relay")]

The [Queen's Baton Relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Baton_Relay "Queen's Baton Relay") was inaugurated at the [Buckingham Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace "Buckingham Palace") on 29 October 2009. The baton, containing a message from [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II") to the athletes, visited 69 Commonwealth nations before reaching India.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-34) It arrived in India on 25 June 2010 through the [Wagah Border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagah_Border "Wagah Border") crossing from Pakistan.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-35) The baton was designed by Foley Design studio and was created by [Titan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_Company "Titan Company") in collaboration with [Bharat Electronics Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharat_Electronics_Limited "Bharat Electronics Limited"). The 664 mm (26.1 in)-high baton weighed 1.9 kg (4.2 lb), and consisted of a triangular section of [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium "Aluminium") twisted into a [helix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helix "Helix") shape and then coated with soils collected from various regions of India. A jewel-encrusted box was used to house the Queen's message, which was laser-engraved onto a 18 carat [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") leaf. The baton was illuminated by several [LEDs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LED "LED"), capable of producing various illuminated designs.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-36)

### Opening ceremony

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Opening ceremony")]

Main article: [2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/A_spectacular_view_of_Jawahar_Lal_Nehru_stadium_during_the_opening_ceremony_of_the_19th_Commonwealth_Games_2010-Delhi%2C_in_New_Delhi_on_October_03%2C_2010_%281%29.jpg/250px-A_spectacular_view_of_Jawahar_Lal_Nehru_stadium_during_the_opening_ceremony_of_the_19th_Commonwealth_Games_2010-Delhi%2C_in_New_Delhi_on_October_03%2C_2010_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:A_spectacular_view_of_Jawahar_Lal_Nehru_stadium_during_the_opening_ceremony_of_the_19th_Commonwealth_Games_2010-Delhi,_in_New_Delhi_on_October_03,_2010_(1).jpg)

[Opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2010 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony") at the [Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru_Stadium_(Delhi) "Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium (Delhi)")

The opening ceremony was held at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium, the main stadium of the event. It began at 19:00[IST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Standard_Time "Indian Standard Time") on 3 October.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-37) The opening ceremony was directed by [Bharat Bala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharat_Bala "Bharat Bala"). It featured over 8,000 performers, and lasted for two-and-a-half hours.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-38) It was estimated to have costed ₹3.5 billion (equivalent to ₹7.9 billion or US$82 million in 2023).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-39)

The ceremony was divided into six separate segments, each showcasing the diverse cultures of India. The countdown took place on the large screen in the stadium, and was accompanied by [fireworks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireworks "Fireworks"). The centerpiece of the ceremony was the helium [aerostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerostat "Aerostat"), which acted as a giant 360° screen for spectators. It began with a showcase of a variety of [drummers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drummer "Drummer") from all parts of India, accompanied by seven-year-old [tabla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabla "Tabla") player. The ceremony showcased a fusion of various classical dances from all parts of India, [mehendi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehendi "Mehendi") decorations, sand paintings, and [yoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoga "Yoga"). The title song was performed by [A. R. Rahman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._R._Rahman "A. R. Rahman"), and singer [Hariharan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hariharan_(singer) "Hariharan (singer)") sang the welcome song for the Games, titled "Swagatam", along with thousands of school children.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-40)

[Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III "Charles III"), the [Prince of Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Wales "Prince of Wales") (representing Elizabeth II as the [Head of the Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_of_the_Commonwealth "Head of the Commonwealth")) and [Pratibha Patil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pratibha_Patil "Pratibha Patil"), the [President of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_India "President of India"), officially declared the Games open.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-41)[Manmohan Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manmohan_Singh "Manmohan Singh"), the [Prime Minister of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India"), and three [heads of state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heads_of_state "Heads of state")–[Mohamed Nasheed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Nasheed "Mohamed Nasheed"), the [President of the Maldives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Maldives "President of the Maldives"), [Marcus Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Stephen "Marcus Stephen"), the [President of Nauru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Nauru "President of Nauru"), [Albert II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_II,_Prince_of_Monaco "Albert II, Prince of Monaco"), the [Prince of Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Monaco "Prince of Monaco"), and [Anand Satyanand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anand_Satyanand "Anand Satyanand"), the [Governor General of New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_General_of_New_Zealand "Governor General of New Zealand"), attended the ceremony.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-43)

## Participating teams

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Participating teams")]

There were 71 participating Commonwealth Games Associations at the 2010 Commonwealth Games. As [Fiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji_at_the_Commonwealth_Games "Fiji at the Commonwealth Games") was suspended from the Commonwealth, it was banned from participating in the Games.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-48) Rwanda fielded a team in the Commonwealth Games for the first time, after becoming a Commonwealth member in 2009.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-49)

Note: The numbers of athletes from each participating association is shown in brackets.

[Kabaddi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaddi "Kabaddi") was a demonstration sport at the Games.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-118)[Triathlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triathlon "Triathlon") was excluded from the Games as there was no suitable location to conduct the swimming stage of the competition.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-119)[Basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") was excluded, while [archery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archery "Archery"), [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis"), and [wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestling "Wrestling"), which were not contested in the 2006 Commonwealth Games, made a comeback.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-120) Despite popular demand, [Cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket") was not included, as the [Board of Control for Cricket in India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Control_for_Cricket_in_India "Board of Control for Cricket in India") were not keen on a [Twenty20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty20 "Twenty20") tournament, and the Games organisers did not want a [one day tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_day_tournament "One day tournament").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-121)

[India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") hosted the 2010 Commonwealth Games which were held in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi") from 3 to 14 October 2010. India won 101 medals in total, including 38 Gold medals, enabling it to finish the Games at second position behind [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"). For the first time in the history of the Games India won over 100 medals in total. For the first time in the history of the Games, India won a medal in [Gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics "Gymnastics"), where [Ashish Kumar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashish_Kumar_(gymnast) "Ashish Kumar (gymnast)") won a Silver and a Bronze. And it was after a gap of 52 years that India won a Gold in Athletics when [Krishna Poonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krishna_Poonia "Krishna Poonia") won Gold in [Women's discus throw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_discus_throw "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's discus throw") and when [Geeta Phogat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geeta_Phogat "Geeta Phogat") won India's first ever gold medal in women's wrestling.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-2)

[India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") hosted the 2010 Commonwealth Games which were held in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi") from 3 to 14 October 2010. India won 101 medals in total, including 38 Gold medals, enabling it to finish the Games at second position behind [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"). For the first time in the history of the Games India won over 100 medals in total. For the first time in the history of the Games, India won a medal in [Gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics "Gymnastics"), where [Ashish Kumar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashish_Kumar_(gymnast) "Ashish Kumar (gymnast)") won a Silver and a Bronze. And it was after a gap of 52 years that India won a Gold in Athletics when [Krishna Poonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krishna_Poonia "Krishna Poonia") won Gold in [Women's discus throw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_discus_throw "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's discus throw") and when [Geeta Phogat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geeta_Phogat "Geeta Phogat") won India's first ever gold medal in women's wrestling.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-2)

# Padma Bhushan Award

## Dhyan Chand

Dhyan Chand was the greatest player the sport has known. His astounding skills have been glorified in various apocryphal stories and anecdotes. A number of such legends revolve around the fact that he had a magical control over dribbling the ball.

He played as the centre forward at three Olympic Games for India winning Gold Medals at Amsterdam in 1928, Los Angeles in 1932 and Berlin in 1936 where he was the captain.

He was a member of the first Indian overseas army team that toured New Zealand in 1926. The team played 21 matches and scored 192 goals with Dhyan Chand scoring over one hundred.

At the Amsterdam Olympics he scored twice as India beat the Netherlands 3-0 in the final.

Four years later at the Los Angeles Olympics India defeated USA 24-1 with Dhyan Chand bagging eight.

At the Berlin Olympics, India cruised to the final beating Hungary 4-0, USA 7-0, Japan 9-0 and France 10-0. In the final against Germany, India scored only once until half time. During the break the maestro removed his shoes to play barefoot and guide India to an emphatic 8-1 victory.

The wizard kept playing till the age of 42 and was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1956.

The country celebrates his birthday, 29 August, as National Sports Day when the President of India gives away all sports awards.

# Padma Bhushan Award

## Dhyan Chand

Dhyan Chand was the greatest player the sport has known. His astounding skills have been glorified in various apocryphal stories and anecdotes. A number of such legends revolve around the fact that he had a magical control over dribbling the ball.

He played as the centre forward at three Olympic Games for India winning Gold Medals at Amsterdam in 1928, Los Angeles in 1932 and Berlin in 1936 where he was the captain.

He was a member of the first Indian overseas army team that toured New Zealand in 1926. The team played 21 matches and scored 192 goals with Dhyan Chand scoring over one hundred.

At the Amsterdam Olympics he scored twice as India beat the Netherlands 3-0 in the final.

Four years later at the Los Angeles Olympics India defeated USA 24-1 with Dhyan Chand bagging eight.

At the Berlin Olympics, India cruised to the final beating Hungary 4-0, USA 7-0, Japan 9-0 and France 10-0. In the final against Germany, India scored only once until half time. During the break the maestro removed his shoes to play barefoot and guide India to an emphatic 8-1 victory.

The wizard kept playing till the age of 42 and was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1956.

The country celebrates his birthday, 29 August, as National Sports Day when the President of India gives away all sports awards.

A A A

> **_From 1954 to 2019, a total of 234 civilian awards (Padma Awards & Bharat Ratna) were given to sportspersons. Cricketers won close to 24% of these awards, 56 to be precise. The only Bharat Ratna to a sportsperson was conferred on Sachin Tendulkar. 35 awards went to Mountaineers while 25 awards went to **\_Hockey players.\_**Sachin Tendulkar & Vishwanathan Anand won three different awards each while the most number of awardees (34) came from Maharashtra._**
> 
> [orc]
> Padma Awards are the[Civilian awards conferred by the Government of India.](https://mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/Scheme-PadmaAwards-050514.pdf)They are given in three categories, namely, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri. On the other hand, [Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian award](https://mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/Scheme-BR_1.pdf) of the country. The Awards are given to individuals who excel in various disciplines like art, social work, public affairs, science and engineering, trade and industry, medicine, literature and education, sports, civil service, etc. ‘Padma Vibhushan’ is awarded for exceptional and distinguished service; ‘Padma Bhushan’ for distinguished service of high order and ‘Padma Shri’ for distinguished service in any field. The Bharat Ratna is awarded in recognition of exceptional service/performance of the highest order in any field of human endeavour. The awards are announced on the occasion of Republic Day every year.
> 
> 
> **Padma Awards to Sportspersons**  
>  Padma Awards were given to individuals who excelled in the[field of Sports since their inception in 1954.](https://mha.gov.in/media/awards-medals) A total of 234 Padma Awards (including one Bharat Ratna) were given to Sportspersons between 1954 and 2019. Of them, 200 are the Padma Shri, 30 are the Padma Bhushan, 3 are the Padma Vibhushan & one the Bharat Ratna. Sachin Tendulkar received the Bharat Ratna, while he along with Vishwanathan Anand & Edmund Hillary received the Padma Vibhushan in the year 2008. Padma awards were given to individuals from 32 different sports. At least two or more awards were given to individuals from 17 different sports while only one award was given to individuals from 15 different sports.  
> ![Image 10](https://factly.in/wp-content/uploads//2019/02/Padma-Awards-Sports-up-to-2019.png)  
> **Cricketers lead the pack**  
>  Out of 234 awards given to sportspersons, 56 went to Cricketers, 35 to Mountaineers, 25 to Hockey Players, 23 to Athletes, 11 to Tennis players, 10 to Badminton players, 10 to Wrestlers, 7 to Chess players, 6 each to Boxers, Billiards players & Football players, 5 each to Swimmers & Shooters. In all, about 24% of all the awards went to Cricketers. Most of the 35 awardees in Mountaineering are from the North East. Cricket, Mountaineering, Hockey & Athletics together accounted for close to 60% of the awards to Sportspersons. Though the Indian Hockey team won a total of eight Olympic gold medals, only 25 Hockey players were given these awards till date, less than half of the awards to Cricketers.  
> ![Image 11](https://factly.in/wp-content/uploads//2019/02/Sportwise-Padma-awards-up-to-2019-.png)**The Top 4 Sports by Awards won**  
>  Cricketers were given the highest number of awards in all the four categories. Among Cricketers who were given these awards, 43 were given Padma Shri, 11 Padma Bhushan , one Padma Vibhushan and one Bharat Ratna. Among Mountaineers, 29 were given Padma Shri, 5 Padma Bhushan and one Padma Vibhushan. Among the Hockey players, 24 were given Padma Shri and one Padma Bhushan to Dhyan Chand. All the 23 awards given to Athletes are Padma Shri.  
> ![Image 12](https://factly.in/wp-content/uploads//2019/02/Top-four-sports-Padma-awards-up-to-2019.png)  
> **Who won the Highest Number of Awards?**  
>  A total of 15 individuals won at least two such awards. Sachin Tendulkar and Vishwanathan Anand are the only ones to have won 3 awards each. Six (6) of these fourteen (14) people are Cricketers, 3 are Mountaineers & 2 are Tennis players. (BR – Bharat Ratna, PV- Padma Vibhushan, PB- Padma Bhushan, PS – Padma Shri)
>

> | Sachin Tendulkar | Cricket | 3 | BR,PV,PS |
> | Vishwanathan Anand | Chess | 3 | PV,PB,PS |
> | Kapil Dev | Cricket | 2 | PB,PS |

> | Pullela Gopichand | Badminton | 2 | PB,PS |
> | D B Deodhar | Cricket | 2 | PB,PS |
> | M C Mary Kom | Boxing | 2 | PB,PS |
> | Nawang Gombu | Mountaineering | 2 | PB,PS |
> | Ramanathan Krishnan | Tennis | 2 | PB,PS |
> | Sonam Gyatso | Mountaineering | 2 | PB,PS |
> | Pankaj Advani | Billiards | 2 | PB,PS |

> | Bachendri Pal | Mountaineering | 2 | PB,PS |
> 
> **Most number of Awardees from Maharashtra**  
>  Only 9 states have at least 10 awardees who are Sportspersons. Topping this list is Maharashtra with 34 awardees followed by Delhi (29), West Bengal (20), Punjab (16), Karnataka (16) ,Tamil Nadu (16), Haryana (15) and Telangana (14) in that order. Close to half the awardees from Maharashtra are Cricketers.

A A A

> **_From 1954 to 2019, a total of 234 civilian awards (Padma Awards & Bharat Ratna) were given to sportspersons. Cricketers won close to 24% of these awards, 56 to be precise. The only Bharat Ratna to a sportsperson was conferred on Sachin Tendulkar. 35 awards went to Mountaineers while 25 awards went to **\_Hockey players.\_**Sachin Tendulkar & Vishwanathan Anand won three different awards each while the most number of awardees (34) came from Maharashtra._**
> 
> [orc]
> Padma Awards are the[Civilian awards conferred by the Government of India.](https://mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/Scheme-PadmaAwards-050514.pdf)They are given in three categories, namely, Padma Vibhushan, Padma Bhushan and Padma Shri. On the other hand, [Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian award](https://mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/Scheme-BR_1.pdf) of the country. The Awards are given to individuals who excel in various disciplines like art, social work, public affairs, science and engineering, trade and industry, medicine, literature and education, sports, civil service, etc. ‘Padma Vibhushan’ is awarded for exceptional and distinguished service; ‘Padma Bhushan’ for distinguished service of high order and ‘Padma Shri’ for distinguished service in any field. The Bharat Ratna is awarded in recognition of exceptional service/performance of the highest order in any field of human endeavour. The awards are announced on the occasion of Republic Day every year.
> 
> 
> **Padma Awards to Sportspersons**  
>  Padma Awards were given to individuals who excelled in the[field of Sports since their inception in 1954.](https://mha.gov.in/media/awards-medals) A total of 234 Padma Awards (including one Bharat Ratna) were given to Sportspersons between 1954 and 2019. Of them, 200 are the Padma Shri, 30 are the Padma Bhushan, 3 are the Padma Vibhushan & one the Bharat Ratna. Sachin Tendulkar received the Bharat Ratna, while he along with Vishwanathan Anand & Edmund Hillary received the Padma Vibhushan in the year 2008. Padma awards were given to individuals from 32 different sports. At least two or more awards were given to individuals from 17 different sports while only one award was given to individuals from 15 different sports.  
> ![Image 10](https://factly.in/wp-content/uploads//2019/02/Padma-Awards-Sports-up-to-2019.png)  
> **Cricketers lead the pack**  
>  Out of 234 awards given to sportspersons, 56 went to Cricketers, 35 to Mountaineers, 25 to Hockey Players, 23 to Athletes, 11 to Tennis players, 10 to Badminton players, 10 to Wrestlers, 7 to Chess players, 6 each to Boxers, Billiards players & Football players, 5 each to Swimmers & Shooters. In all, about 24% of all the awards went to Cricketers. Most of the 35 awardees in Mountaineering are from the North East. Cricket, Mountaineering, Hockey & Athletics together accounted for close to 60% of the awards to Sportspersons. Though the Indian Hockey team won a total of eight Olympic gold medals, only 25 Hockey players were given these awards till date, less than half of the awards to Cricketers.  
> ![Image 11](https://factly.in/wp-content/uploads//2019/02/Sportwise-Padma-awards-up-to-2019-.png)**The Top 4 Sports by Awards won**  
>  Cricketers were given the highest number of awards in all the four categories. Among Cricketers who were given these awards, 43 were given Padma Shri, 11 Padma Bhushan , one Padma Vibhushan and one Bharat Ratna. Among Mountaineers, 29 were given Padma Shri, 5 Padma Bhushan and one Padma Vibhushan. Among the Hockey players, 24 were given Padma Shri and one Padma Bhushan to Dhyan Chand. All the 23 awards given to Athletes are Padma Shri.  
> ![Image 12](https://factly.in/wp-content/uploads//2019/02/Top-four-sports-Padma-awards-up-to-2019.png)  
> **Who won the Highest Number of Awards?**  
>  A total of 15 individuals won at least two such awards. Sachin Tendulkar and Vishwanathan Anand are the only ones to have won 3 awards each. Six (6) of these fourteen (14) people are Cricketers, 3 are Mountaineers & 2 are Tennis players. (BR – Bharat Ratna, PV- Padma Vibhushan, PB- Padma Bhushan, PS – Padma Shri)

# Padma Awards 2026: Vijay Amritraj conferred Padma Bhushan; Rohit Sharma, Harmanpreet Kaur get Padma Shri - sports winners list

Indian hockey goalkeeper Savita Punia too earned the Padma Shri while Vladimir Mestvirishvili of Georgia was honoured posthumously for his contribution to wrestling.

![Image 2: GettyImages-2241971963](https://img.olympics.com/images/image/private/t_s_16_9_g_auto/t_s_w1460/f_auto/primary/i7td2j6duiuuio19i6xp)

Picture by 2025 Getty Images

By Andre Pitts 25 January 2026 14:31 GMT+0 4 min read

World Cup-winning [Indian cricket team captains](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/india-cricket-team-t20-captain-list-men-women)**Rohit Sharma** and **Harmanpreet Kaur** were among nine sportspersons who were conferred with the **Padma Awards 2026** by the Indian government on Sunday.

[Indian tennis](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/best-indian-tennis-players-famous-grand-slams-olympic-games-medal) great **Vijay Amritraj** was conferred with **Padma Bhushan**, while Rohit Sharma, Harmanpreet Kaur and [Indian hockey](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/indian-field-hockey-history-legacy-olympics-world-cup-dhyan-chand-balbir) team goalkeeper Savita Punia received the **Padma Shri** award.

The **Padma Awards** are given to individuals for their distinguished service in any field. The Padma Bhushan is India’s third-highest civilian award after the Bharat Ratna and the Padma Visbhushan. The Padma Shri is the fourth-highest civilian award.

A trailblazer in Indian [tennis](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/tennis-rules-regulations-how-to-play-basics), Vijay Amritraj represented India at the Seoul 1988 Olympics and reached a career-high ranking of world No. 18 in singles in 1980.

He reached four Grand Slam singles quarter-finals - twice each at Wimbledon (1973 and 1981) and at the US Open (1973 and 1974).

A 15-time winner on the ATP Tour as a singles player, Vijay Amritraj also had several big scalps to his name, including a win over Björn Borg at the 1974 US Open and tennis icon John McEnroe at the 1984 Cincinnati Masters.

Partnering with brother Anand Amritraj, Vijay also won 13 ATP titles and reached the semi-finals of the 1976 Wimbledon, where they lost to eventual champions, Brian Gottfried and Raul Ramirez.

Cricketer Rohit Sharma received the Padma Shri award after title winning campaigns as captain for India at the [T20 World Cup](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/t20-world-cup-winners-list-champions) 2024 and the Champions Trophy 2025.

Harmanpreet Kaur also received the Padma Shri award after guiding the Indian women’s cricket team to their maiden [ODI World Cup](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/women-cricket-world-cup-winners-list) title last year.

Two-time Olympian Savita Punia, who was India women’s hockey team’s vice-captain during their historic fourth-placed finish at Tokyo 2020, also received the Padma Shri. She is also the second Indian goalkeeper, after PR Sreejesh, to complete 300 international caps.

A former captain of the Indian women’s hockey team, Savita led the side to a bronze medal at the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games and a title-winning campaign at the FIH Nations Cup. With her help, India also clinched back-to-back titles at the Women’s Asian Champions Trophy in 2023 and 2024.

Legendary Georgian [wrestling](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/indian-wrestling-history-legacy-olympics-medals-world-championships) coach Vladimir Mestvirishvili, who trained several Olympic medallists, received a Padma Shri award posthumously. He also became the first foreign coach to receive the Padma Shri.

A mentor to several [Indian wrestlers](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/famous-indian-wrestlers-list), Vladimir Mestvirishvili trained Olympic medal winners [Yogeshwar Dutt](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/who-yogeshwar-dutt-london-2012-olympics-medal-bronze-indian-wrestler), [Sushil Kumar](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/sushil-kumar-london-2012-olympics-silver-medal-indian-wrestler), [Ravi Dahiya](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/ravi-kumar-dahiya-tokyo-olympics-silver-medal-india-wrestling) and [Bajrang Punia](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/bajrang-punia-olympics-medal-tokyo-2020-wrestling). He died last year at the age of 81.

Baldev Singh received the Padma Shri for his service to [hockey](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/field-hockey-rules-how-to-play) both as a player and a coach. He represented India at the Montreal 1976 Olympics and featured in three [Hockey World Cups](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/fih-hockey-world-cup-winners-list-champions). He is also a two-time Asian Games silver medallist.

Following his playing career,Baldev Singh emerged as one of the most influential coaches in Indian hockey, shaping the international careers of numerous players, many of whom went on to represent India at the highest level.

Among his most prominent proteges are Olympic medallist and former drag-flick specialist Sandeep Singh, former India women’s captain Rani Rampal, along with Didar Singh, Sanjeev Kumar Dang, Harpal Singh and Navjot Kaur.

For his immense contribution to coaching and player development, he was conferred with the [Dronacharya Award](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/dronacharya-award-given-india-coaches-excellence-first-recipient) in 2009.

*   Vladimir Mestvirishvili (Posthumous) - Padma Shri

# Padma Awards 2026: Vijay Amritraj conferred Padma Bhushan; Rohit Sharma, Harmanpreet Kaur get Padma Shri - sports winners list

Indian hockey goalkeeper Savita Punia too earned the Padma Shri while Vladimir Mestvirishvili of Georgia was honoured posthumously for his contribution to wrestling.

![Image 2: GettyImages-2241971963](https://img.olympics.com/images/image/private/t_s_16_9_g_auto/t_s_w1460/f_auto/primary/i7td2j6duiuuio19i6xp)

Picture by 2025 Getty Images

By Andre Pitts 25 January 2026 14:31 GMT+0 4 min read

World Cup-winning [Indian cricket team captains](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/india-cricket-team-t20-captain-list-men-women)**Rohit Sharma** and **Harmanpreet Kaur** were among nine sportspersons who were conferred with the **Padma Awards 2026** by the Indian government on Sunday.

[Indian tennis](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/best-indian-tennis-players-famous-grand-slams-olympic-games-medal) great **Vijay Amritraj** was conferred with **Padma Bhushan**, while Rohit Sharma, Harmanpreet Kaur and [Indian hockey](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/indian-field-hockey-history-legacy-olympics-world-cup-dhyan-chand-balbir) team goalkeeper Savita Punia received the **Padma Shri** award.

The **Padma Awards** are given to individuals for their distinguished service in any field. The Padma Bhushan is India’s third-highest civilian award after the Bharat Ratna and the Padma Visbhushan. The Padma Shri is the fourth-highest civilian award.

A trailblazer in Indian [tennis](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/tennis-rules-regulations-how-to-play-basics), Vijay Amritraj represented India at the Seoul 1988 Olympics and reached a career-high ranking of world No. 18 in singles in 1980.

He reached four Grand Slam singles quarter-finals - twice each at Wimbledon (1973 and 1981) and at the US Open (1973 and 1974).

A 15-time winner on the ATP Tour as a singles player, Vijay Amritraj also had several big scalps to his name, including a win over Björn Borg at the 1974 US Open and tennis icon John McEnroe at the 1984 Cincinnati Masters.

Partnering with brother Anand Amritraj, Vijay also won 13 ATP titles and reached the semi-finals of the 1976 Wimbledon, where they lost to eventual champions, Brian Gottfried and Raul Ramirez.

Cricketer Rohit Sharma received the Padma Shri award after title winning campaigns as captain for India at the [T20 World Cup](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/t20-world-cup-winners-list-champions) 2024 and the Champions Trophy 2025.

Harmanpreet Kaur also received the Padma Shri award after guiding the Indian women’s cricket team to their maiden [ODI World Cup](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/women-cricket-world-cup-winners-list) title last year.

Two-time Olympian Savita Punia, who was India women’s hockey team’s vice-captain during their historic fourth-placed finish at Tokyo 2020, also received the Padma Shri. She is also the second Indian goalkeeper, after PR Sreejesh, to complete 300 international caps.

A former captain of the Indian women’s hockey team, Savita led the side to a bronze medal at the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games and a title-winning campaign at the FIH Nations Cup. With her help, India also clinched back-to-back titles at the Women’s Asian Champions Trophy in 2023 and 2024.

Legendary Georgian [wrestling](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/indian-wrestling-history-legacy-olympics-medals-world-championships) coach Vladimir Mestvirishvili, who trained several Olympic medallists, received a Padma Shri award posthumously. He also became the first foreign coach to receive the Padma Shri.

A mentor to several [Indian wrestlers](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/famous-indian-wrestlers-list), Vladimir Mestvirishvili trained Olympic medal winners [Yogeshwar Dutt](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/who-yogeshwar-dutt-london-2012-olympics-medal-bronze-indian-wrestler), [Sushil Kumar](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/sushil-kumar-london-2012-olympics-silver-medal-indian-wrestler), [Ravi Dahiya](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/ravi-kumar-dahiya-tokyo-olympics-silver-medal-india-wrestling) and [Bajrang Punia](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/bajrang-punia-olympics-medal-tokyo-2020-wrestling). He died last year at the age of 81.

Baldev Singh received the Padma Shri for his service to [hockey](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/field-hockey-rules-how-to-play) both as a player and a coach. He represented India at the Montreal 1976 Olympics and featured in three [Hockey World Cups](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/fih-hockey-world-cup-winners-list-champions). He is also a two-time Asian Games silver medallist.

Following his playing career,Baldev Singh emerged as one of the most influential coaches in Indian hockey, shaping the international careers of numerous players, many of whom went on to represent India at the highest level.

Among his most prominent proteges are Olympic medallist and former drag-flick specialist Sandeep Singh, former India women’s captain Rani Rampal, along with Didar Singh, Sanjeev Kumar Dang, Harpal Singh and Navjot Kaur.

For his immense contribution to coaching and player development, he was conferred with the [Dronacharya Award](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/dronacharya-award-given-india-coaches-excellence-first-recipient) in 2009.

*   Baldev Singh - Padma Shri

*   Bhagwandas Raikwar - Padma Shri

*   Harmanpreet Kaur - Padma Shri

*   K Pajanivel - Padma Shri

*   Praveen Kumar - Padma Shri

*   Rohit Sharma - Padma Shri

*   Savita Punia - Padma Shri

*   Vladimir Mestvirishvili (Posthumous) - Padma Shri

 #### [16. Kapil Dev](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1337956/?ref_=ls_t_16) 

    *   Actor

['83 (2021)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt7518786/?ref_=ls_knf_16)

Believe it or not, this tall, muscular, forever smiling lad from Chandigarh, at a camp for emerging Indian cricketers, was denied extra food during lunch. When asked by the camp authorities why he requested for more than the standard quota, he stated that being a fast bowler he needs to eat more to maintain stamina. The camp burst into laughter, with the response from the coaches being "We don't produce fast-bowlers in India". Rest as the cliche goes is history.  
  
Starting from his debut in 1978, where he delivered a bouncer to arch-rivals Pakistan's opening batsmen, till his retirement in 1994, Kapil Dev sent back several of cricket history's best batsmen against pace bowling back to the pavilion, even on the unhelpful wickets of his home country, displaying his ability to think players out with a combination of consistent line and length as well as swinging the ball both inside and outside of the wicket. This formed the core of his outstanding tally of 434 test and 253 ODI scalps, both stats being world records at the time of him bowing out.  
  
And if the bowling alone wasn't enough, his batting displays became box-office attractions the world over, particularly against the best bowling attacks of his generation. Although always criticized for just enjoying batting in a destructive mode rather than being an accumulator like his cross border rival Imran Khan, he did more than enough to reach over 5000 runs with 8 centuries, 3 of which came outside the subcontinent. And his only ODI ton may very well arguably be the greatest innings in the history of the format, with his 175* against Zimbabwe in the 1983 World Cup won the match, saved India from crashing out of the Group Stages unlike the previous two editions and above all India beat the mighty West Indies to clinch their first ever ICC tournament. An icing on the cake, Kapil happened to be the captain of this side which pulled off the impossible, his contributions being in both batting and bowling as well as fielding, as evidenced during the finals by his backwards running catch to dismiss Sir Viv Richards and the blinder to get rid of West Indian captain Clive Lloyd.  
  
His tenure as a coach of the national team, however, was mediocre to say the least and allegations of match-fixing were raised against him by former teammate Manoj Prabhakar, forcing him to disappear from public life for a while. Cleared of all charges after thorough investigation, Kapil returned to public eye and in 2002 was voted by Wisden as India's "Cricketer Of The 20th Century" ahead of long time teammate Sunil Gavaskar and crowd favorite Sachin Tendulkar, the honor presented to him by his friend and batting legend Sir Vivian Richards.  
  
Today, Kapil Dev continues to remain a revered figure in the international cricket community, with his name always popping up whenever someone thinks of the term "all-rounder" and is unsurprisingly a prominent guest lecturer on leadership and team management at events held on several prominent university and college campuses in India.  
  
God bless the "Haryana Hurricane".

Dev is the only player in the history of cricket to have taken more than 400 wickets (434 wickets) and scored more than 5,000 runs in Test. Dev captained the Indian cricket team that won the 1983 Cricket World Cup.

A near to flawless batting technique, unmatched patience when on the crease and an insane appetite for runs combined together made Sunil Manohar Gavaskar. Born in Mumbai in 1949, Gavaskar proved to be a batting prodigy in the first class circuit, leading to his international debut on the tour of the Caribbean in 1971. What most expected from the little man was a steady stream of runs. But what they got, was a non-stop cascade as he ended the series with 774 runs at a whooping average of 155. All of a sudden, Gavaskar was a subject of immense curiosity in the international cricket community. But following his unreal debut, the following couple of seasons were mediocre to say the least. Questions started to be raised if Gavaskar's feats in his debut series were a fluke. But larger-than-life as Gavaskar was, he proved his cynics wrong hitting a miraculous 101 on a broken Old Trafford pitch against the devastating quartet of Bob Willis, Chris Old, Mike Hendrik and John Snow. Restored to confidence with another storybook accomplishment, Gavaskar was once again the man cricket world admired and bowlers dreaded, displaying a wide array of strokes in all corners of the globe. As the saga continued, Gavaskar kept bringing landmark after landmark to his name, the most immortal ones among them being his 221 in the fourth innings chasing 438 against England at The Oval, overtaking Geoffrey Boycott as the highest run scorer in test history, beating Sir Don Bradman's 35 year old record of 29 test centuries and finally becoming the first cricketer to scale 10000 runs. And his farewell innings in 1987 became another heralded story as batting on a crumbling Bangalore wicket against arch rivals Pakistan, Gavaskar scored 96 in a heartbreaking loss, with the display of India's complete reliance on Gavaskar proven by the fact that the next highest contribution to Indian total was extras conceded by Pakistani bowlers, with 27.  
  
Gavaskar bowed out of the scene with 10122 runs averaging 51, over 9500 of the tally coming as an opener. He had famously said "Others will definitely get there, but the one who gets it first is the one always remembered". True to his words, despite the likes of Sachin Tendulkar and Rahul Dravid having surpassed him by quite a distance, Sunil Gavaskar continues to be regarded, both domestically and internationally, as India's greatest batsman of all-time. After all, the one who sets the benchmark has his own aura, Right !!!!!

Believe it or not, this tall, muscular, forever smiling lad from Chandigarh, at a camp for emerging Indian cricketers, was denied extra food during lunch. When asked by the camp authorities why he requested for more than the standard quota, he stated that being a fast bowler he needs to eat more to maintain stamina. The camp burst into laughter, with the response from the coaches being "We don't produce fast-bowlers in India". Rest as the cliche goes is history.  
  
Starting from his debut in 1978, where he delivered a bouncer to arch-rivals Pakistan's opening batsmen, till his retirement in 1994, Kapil Dev sent back several of cricket history's best batsmen against pace bowling back to the pavilion, even on the unhelpful wickets of his home country, displaying his ability to think players out with a combination of consistent line and length as well as swinging the ball both inside and outside of the wicket. And if the bowling alone wasn't enough, his batting displays became box-office attractions the world over, particularly against the best bowling attacks of his generation. Although always criticized for just enjoying batting in a destructive mode rather than being an accumulator like his cross border rival Imran Khan, he did more than enough to reach over 5000 runs with 8 centuries, 3 of which came outside the subcontinent. And his only ODI ton may very well arguably be the greatest innings in the history of the format, with his 175* against Zimbabwe in the 1983 World Cup won the match, saved India from crashing out of the Group Stages unlike the previous two editions and above all India beat the mighty West Indies to clinch their first ever ICC tournament. An icing on the cake, Kapil happened to be the captain of this side which pulled off the impossible, his contributions being in both batting and bowling as well as fielding, as evidenced during the finals by his backwards running catch to dismiss Sir Viv Richards and the blinder to get rid of West Indian captain Clive Lloyd.  
  
His tenure as a coach of the national team, however, was mediocre to say the least and allegations of match-fixing were raised against him by former teammate Manoj Prabhakar, forcing him to disappear from public life for a while. Cleared of all charges after thorough investigation, Kapil returned to public eye and in 2002 was voted by Wisden as India's "Cricketer Of The 20th Century" ahead of long time teammate Sunil Gavaskar and crowd favorite Sachin Tendulkar, the honor presented to him by his friend and batting legend Sir Vivian Richards.  
  
Today, Kapil Dev continues to remain a revered figure in the international cricket community, with his name always popping up whenever someone thinks of the term "all-rounder" and is unsurprisingly a prominent guest lecturer on leadership and team management at events held on several prominent university and college campuses in India.  
  
God bless the "Haryana Hurricane".

Dev is the only player in the history of cricket to have taken more than 400 wickets (434 wickets) and scored more than 5,000 runs in Test. Dev captained the Indian cricket team that won the 1983 Cricket World Cup.

A near to flawless batting technique, unmatched patience when on the crease and an insane appetite for runs combined together made Sunil Manohar Gavaskar. Born in Mumbai in 1949, Gavaskar proved to be a batting prodigy in the first class circuit, leading to his international debut on the tour of the Caribbean in 1971. What most expected from the little man was a steady stream of runs. But what they got, was a non-stop cascade as he ended the series with 774 runs at a whooping average of 155. All of a sudden, Gavaskar was a subject of immense curiosity in the international cricket community. But following his unreal debut, the following couple of seasons were mediocre to say the least. Questions started to be raised if Gavaskar's feats in his debut series were a fluke. But larger-than-life as Gavaskar was, he proved his cynics wrong hitting a miraculous 101 on a broken Old Trafford pitch against the devastating quartet of Bob Willis, Chris Old, Mike Hendrik and John Snow. Restored to confidence with another storybook accomplishment, Gavaskar was once again the man cricket world admired and bowlers dreaded, displaying a wide array of strokes in all corners of the globe. As the saga continued, Gavaskar kept bringing landmark after landmark to his name, the most immortal ones among them being his 221 in the fourth innings chasing 438 against England at The Oval, overtaking Geoffrey Boycott as the highest run scorer in test history, beating Sir Don Bradman's 35 year old record of 29 test centuries and finally becoming the first cricketer to scale 10000 runs. And his farewell innings in 1987 became another heralded story as batting on a crumbling Bangalore wicket against arch rivals Pakistan, Gavaskar scored 96 in a heartbreaking loss, with the display of India's complete reliance on Gavaskar proven by the fact that the next highest contribution to Indian total was extras conceded by Pakistani bowlers, with 27.  
  
Gavaskar bowed out of the scene with 10122 runs averaging 51, over 9500 of the tally coming as an opener. He had famously said "Others will definitely get there, but the one who gets it first is the one always remembered". True to his words, despite the likes of Sachin Tendulkar and Rahul Dravid having surpassed him by quite a distance, Sunil Gavaskar continues to be regarded, both domestically and internationally, as India's greatest batsman of all-time. After all, the one who sets the benchmark has his own aura, Right !!!!!

Gavaskar was the first Test cricket player to make over 10,000 runs and first player to score 30 centuries
