Rahul Dravid](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1340409/?ref_=ls_t_39) [Stumped (2003)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0357208/?ref_=ls_knf_39)     In the game of cricket, some judge batsmen by the number of runs they make while some are judged based on the manner and in the circumstances they are made. By either criteria, with both formats in mind, Rahul Sharad Dravid is unarguably one of the greatest of all-time.  
  
The son of a food scientist and a professor of architecture, Dravid represented the state of Karnataka in the Indian Domestic Circuit. With years of consistent performances, he finally made it to the 1996 Indian touring party for England. When told by coach Sandeep Patil that he would finally get to bat at Lord's, his face just lit up. Joining fellow debutante and future skipper Saurav Ganguly, Dravid made highly polished, textbook strokes before unfortunately falling for 95. During the following years, Dravid maintained high levels of his trademark consistency but wasn't able to convert fifties into centuries. This dilemma came to an end at Johannesburg, when against pace legend Allan Donald at his peak, he registered scores of 148 and 81. From there on, there was no looking back. And entering into the 21st century, Dravid became the centrefold of India's batting line-up, with India finally starting to win tests overseas, Dravid trailing only Sachin Tendulkar for the title of India's greatest batsman ever.  
  
But like all greats, Dravid too lost form in the middle years starting from India's disastrous exit from the 2007 World Cup. Working hard to remodel his technique, Dravid finally found his touch on India's otherwise disastrous tour of England in 2011 where despite his 3 centuries, India was whitewashed 4-0. And after an individual poor showing in another 4-0 series whitewash, this time in Australia, Dravid, knowing fully both cricket viewers and critics will come for his blood, announced his retirement from international cricket.  
  
"The Wall", as he is fondly called by the global cricket community, continues to contribute to India as one of the guiding lights to youngsters, nurturing their skills before they become the mainstray of the National team.  
  
One of the nicest men to ever grace the sport, Dravid has unquestionably carved his name as one of the greatest of all-time.

## About Padma Vibhushan Award Winners in Sports

 The Padma Vibhushan is the second-highest civilian award of the Republic of India, after the Bharat Ratna. Instituted on 2 January 1954, the award is given for "exceptional and distinguished service". All persons without distinction of race, occupation, position or sex are eligible for these awards. 

## History of Padma Vibhushan Award Winners in Sports

 Only four sportspersons have ever received the Padma Vibhushan, India's second-highest civilian honor, underscoring how exclusive this category is compared to fields like literature, science, or public affairs. Chess grandmaster Viswanathan Anand and cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar both received it in 2008, the same year New Zealand mountaineer Sir Edmund Hillary was honored posthumously for his 1953 Everest ascent. Boxer M. C. Mary Kom, a six-time world champion, was recognized in 2020, becoming the first female athlete to earn this rare distinction.

## About Padma Vibhushan Award Winners in Sports

 The Padma Vibhushan is the second-highest civilian award of the Republic of India, after the Bharat Ratna. Instituted on 2 January 1954, the award is given for "exceptional and distinguished service". All persons without distinction of race, occupation, position or sex are eligible for these awards. 

## History of Padma Vibhushan Award Winners in Sports

 Only four sportspersons have ever received the Padma Vibhushan, India's second-highest civilian honor, underscoring how exclusive this category is compared to fields like literature, science, or public affairs. Chess grandmaster Viswanathan Anand and cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar both received it in 2008, the same year New Zealand mountaineer Sir Edmund Hillary was honored posthumously for his 1953 Everest ascent. Boxer M. C. Mary Kom, a six-time world champion, was recognized in 2020, becoming the first female athlete to earn this rare distinction.

The [Padma Vibhushan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Vibhushan "Padma Vibhushan") is the second highest [civilian award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_honours_system "Indian honours system") of the [Republic of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"). Instituted on 2 January 1954,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1954-1) the award is given for the "exceptional and distinguished service", without distinction of race, occupation, position, or sex. The Padma Vibhushan award recipients are announced every year on [Republic Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Day_(India) "Republic Day (India)") and registered in _[The Gazette of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gazette\_of\_India "The Gazette of India")_—a publication released weekly by the Department of Publication, [Ministry of Urban Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Housing_and_Urban_Affairs "Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs") used for official government notices.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2) The conferral of the award is not considered official without its publication in the _Gazette_. Recipients whose awards have been revoked or restored, both of which require the authority of the President, are also registered in the _Gazette_ and are required to surrender their medals when their names are struck from the register.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1955-3)As of 2020[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients&action=edit), none of the conferments of Padma Vibhushan have been revoked or restored. The recommendations are received from all the state and the union territory governments, the Ministries of the Government, the [Bharat Ratna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharat_Ratna "Bharat Ratna") and previous Padma Vibhushan award recipients, the Institutes of Excellence, the Ministers, the [Chief Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_current_Indian_chief_ministers "List of current Indian chief ministers") and the [Governors of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_current_Indian_governors "List of current Indian governors"), and the Members of Parliament including private individuals. The recommendations received during 1 May and 15 September of every year are submitted to the Padma Awards Committee, constituted by the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India"). The committee recommendations are later submitted to the Prime Minister and the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_India "President of India") for the further approval.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2)

When instituted in 1954, the Padma Vibhushan was classified as "Pahla Varg" (Class I) under the three-tier Padma Vibhushan awards; preceded by the Bharat Ratna, the highest civilian award,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-BRscheme-4) and followed by "Dusra Varg" (Class II), and "Tisra Varg" (Class III).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1954-1) On 15 January 1955, the Padma Vibhushan was reclassified into three different awards; the Padma Vibhushan, the highest of the three, followed by the [Padma Bhushan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Bhushan "Padma Bhushan") and the [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri"). The criteria includes "exceptional and distinguished service in any field including service rendered by Government servants" but excluding those working with the [Public sector undertakings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_sector_undertakings_in_India "Public sector undertakings in India") with the exception of doctors and scientists. The 1954 statutes did not allow posthumous awards but this was subsequently modified in the January 1955 statute.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1955-3) The award, along with other personal [civil honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_honours_system#Civilian_awards "Indian honours system"), was briefly suspended twice in its history;[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoibergRamchandani200096-5) for the first time in July 1977 when [Morarji Desai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morarji_Desai "Morarji Desai") was sworn in as the fourth Prime Minister.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBhattacherje2009A248-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdgar2011C-105-7) The suspension was rescinded on 25 January 1980, after [Indira Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi "Indira Gandhi") became the Prime Minister.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBhattacherje2009A253-8) The civilian awards were suspended again in mid-1992, when two [Public-Interest Litigations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_interest_law "Public interest law") were filed in the [High Courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_High_Courts_of_India "List of High Courts of India") questioning the civilian awards being "Titles" per an interpretation of [Article 18 (1)](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Constitution%20of%20India/Part%20III "s:Constitution of India/Part III") of the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_India "Constitution of India").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoibergRamchandani200096-5)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-Article18-10) The awards were reintroduced by the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_India "Supreme Court of India") in December 1995, following the conclusion of the litigation.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-sci-11)

The recipients receive a _Sanad_ (certificate) signed by the President and a medal with no monetary grant associated with the award.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2) The decoration is a circular-shaped toned bronze medallion 1+3⁄4 inches (44 mm) in diameter and 1⁄8 inch (3.2 mm) thick. The centrally placed pattern made of outer lines of a square of 1+3⁄16 inches (30 mm) side is embossed with a knob embossed within each of the outer angles of the pattern. A raised circular space of diameter 1+1⁄16 inches (27 mm) is placed at the centre of the decoration. A centrally located lotus flower is embossed on the obverse side of the medal and the text "Padma" written in [Devanagari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devanagari "Devanagari") script is placed above and the text "Vibhushan" is placed below the lotus. The [Emblem of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emblem_of_India "Emblem of India") is placed in the centre of the reverse side with the national motto, "[Satyameva Jayate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyameva_Jayate "Satyameva Jayate")" (Truth alone triumphs) in Devanagari Script, inscribed on the lower edge. The rim, the edges and all embossing on either side is of white gold with the text "Padma Vibhushan" of silver gilt. The medal is suspended by a pink riband 1+1⁄4 inches (32 mm) in width.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1955-3) It is ranked fourth in the order of precedence of wearing of medals and decorations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-12)

The first recipients of the Padma Vibhushan were [Satyendra Nath Bose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyendra_Nath_Bose "Satyendra Nath Bose"), [Nandalal Bose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandalal_Bose "Nandalal Bose"), [Zakir Husain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zakir_Husain_(politician) "Zakir Husain (politician)"), [Balasaheb Gangadhar Kher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._G._Kher "B. G. Kher"), [V. K. Krishna Menon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._K._Krishna_Menon "V. K. Krishna Menon"), and [Jigme Dorji Wangchuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigme_Dorji_Wangchuck "Jigme Dorji Wangchuck"), who were honoured in 1954. As of 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients&action=edit), the award has been bestowed on 348 individuals, including thirty-four posthumous and twenty-five non-citizen recipients.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PadmaAwards-13) Some of the recipients have refused or returned their awards; [P. N. Haksar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._N._Haksar "P. N. Haksar"),[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-15)[Vilayat Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilayat_Khan "Vilayat Khan"),[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-18)[E. M. S. Namboodiripad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._M._S._Namboodiripad "E. M. S. Namboodiripad"),[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-20)[Swami Ranganathananda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swami_Ranganathananda "Swami Ranganathananda"),[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-22) and [Manikonda Chalapathi Rau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manikonda_Chalapathi_Rau "Manikonda Chalapathi Rau") refused the award; the family members of [Lakshmi Chand Jain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakshmi_Chand_Jain "Lakshmi Chand Jain") (2011) and [Sharad Anantrao Joshi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharad_Anantrao_Joshi "Sharad Anantrao Joshi") (2016) declined their posthumous conferments,[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-Jain-25)[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-Joshi-27) and 1986 recipient [Baba Amte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baba_Amte "Baba Amte") and 2015 recipient [Parkash Singh Badal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkash_Singh_Badal "Parkash Singh Badal") returned theirs honour in 1991 and 2020 respectively.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-28)[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-Amte-30)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-31)[[i]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-32) The 2026 award was bestowed upon five recipients–[Dharmendra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharmendra "Dharmendra") (posthumous), [K. T. Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K._T._Thomas_(judge) "K. T. Thomas (judge)"), [N. Rajam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N._Rajam "N. Rajam"), [P. Narayanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._Narayanan_(journalist) "P. Narayanan (journalist)"), and [V. S. Achuthanandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Achuthanandan "V. S. Achuthanandan") (posthumous).

The [Padma Vibhushan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Vibhushan "Padma Vibhushan") is the second highest [civilian award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_honours_system "Indian honours system") of the [Republic of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"). Instituted on 2 January 1954,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1954-1) the award is given for the "exceptional and distinguished service", without distinction of race, occupation, position, or sex. The Padma Vibhushan award recipients are announced every year on [Republic Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Day_(India) "Republic Day (India)") and registered in _[The Gazette of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gazette\_of\_India "The Gazette of India")_—a publication released weekly by the Department of Publication, [Ministry of Urban Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Housing_and_Urban_Affairs "Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs") used for official government notices.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2) The conferral of the award is not considered official without its publication in the _Gazette_. Recipients whose awards have been revoked or restored, both of which require the authority of the President, are also registered in the _Gazette_ and are required to surrender their medals when their names are struck from the register.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1955-3)As of 2020[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients&action=edit), none of the conferments of Padma Vibhushan have been revoked or restored. The recommendations are received from all the state and the union territory governments, the Ministries of the Government, the [Bharat Ratna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharat_Ratna "Bharat Ratna") and previous Padma Vibhushan award recipients, the Institutes of Excellence, the Ministers, the [Chief Ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_current_Indian_chief_ministers "List of current Indian chief ministers") and the [Governors of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_current_Indian_governors "List of current Indian governors"), and the Members of Parliament including private individuals. The recommendations received during 1 May and 15 September of every year are submitted to the Padma Awards Committee, constituted by the [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India"). The committee recommendations are later submitted to the Prime Minister and the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_India "President of India") for the further approval.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2)

When instituted in 1954, the Padma Vibhushan was classified as "Pahla Varg" (Class I) under the three-tier Padma Vibhushan awards; preceded by the Bharat Ratna, the highest civilian award,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-BRscheme-4) and followed by "Dusra Varg" (Class II), and "Tisra Varg" (Class III).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1954-1) On 15 January 1955, the Padma Vibhushan was reclassified into three different awards; the Padma Vibhushan, the highest of the three, followed by the [Padma Bhushan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Bhushan "Padma Bhushan") and the [Padma Shri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Padma_Shri "Padma Shri"). The criteria includes "exceptional and distinguished service in any field including service rendered by Government servants" but excluding those working with the [Public sector undertakings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_sector_undertakings_in_India "Public sector undertakings in India") with the exception of doctors and scientists. The 1954 statutes did not allow posthumous awards but this was subsequently modified in the January 1955 statute.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1955-3) The award, along with other personal [civil honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_honours_system#Civilian_awards "Indian honours system"), was briefly suspended twice in its history;[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoibergRamchandani200096-5) for the first time in July 1977 when [Morarji Desai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morarji_Desai "Morarji Desai") was sworn in as the fourth Prime Minister.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBhattacherje2009A248-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdgar2011C-105-7) The suspension was rescinded on 25 January 1980, after [Indira Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indira_Gandhi "Indira Gandhi") became the Prime Minister.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBhattacherje2009A253-8) The civilian awards were suspended again in mid-1992, when two [Public-Interest Litigations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_interest_law "Public interest law") were filed in the [High Courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_High_Courts_of_India "List of High Courts of India") questioning the civilian awards being "Titles" per an interpretation of [Article 18 (1)](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Constitution%20of%20India/Part%20III "s:Constitution of India/Part III") of the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_India "Constitution of India").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoibergRamchandani200096-5)[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-Article18-10) The awards were reintroduced by the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_India "Supreme Court of India") in December 1995, following the conclusion of the litigation.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-sci-11)

The recipients receive a _Sanad_ (certificate) signed by the President and a medal with no monetary grant associated with the award.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-PAscheme-2) The decoration is a circular-shaped toned bronze medallion 1+3⁄4 inches (44 mm) in diameter and 1⁄8 inch (3.2 mm) thick. The centrally placed pattern made of outer lines of a square of 1+3⁄16 inches (30 mm) side is embossed with a knob embossed within each of the outer angles of the pattern. A raised circular space of diameter 1+1⁄16 inches (27 mm) is placed at the centre of the decoration. A centrally located lotus flower is embossed on the obverse side of the medal and the text "Padma" written in [Devanagari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devanagari "Devanagari") script is placed above and the text "Vibhushan" is placed below the lotus. The [Emblem of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emblem_of_India "Emblem of India") is placed in the centre of the reverse side with the national motto, "[Satyameva Jayate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyameva_Jayate "Satyameva Jayate")" (Truth alone triumphs) in Devanagari Script, inscribed on the lower edge. The rim, the edges and all embossing on either side is of white gold with the text "Padma Vibhushan" of silver gilt. The medal is suspended by a pink riband 1+1⁄4 inches (32 mm) in width.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-award1955-3) It is ranked fourth in the order of precedence of wearing of medals and decorations.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Padma_Vibhushan_award_recipients#cite_note-12)

The first recipients of the Padma Vibhushan were [Satyendra Nath Bose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyendra_Nath_Bose "Satyendra Nath Bose"), [Nandalal Bose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandalal_Bose "Nandalal Bose"), [Zakir Husain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zakir_Husain_(politician) "Zakir Husain (politician)"), [Balasaheb Gangadhar Kher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._G._Kher "B. G. Kher"), [V. K. Krishna Menon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._K._Krishna_Menon "V. K. Krishna Menon"), and [Jigme Dorji Wangchuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jigme_Dorji_Wangchuck "Jigme Dorji Wangchuck"), who were honoured in 1954. # Commonwealth Games 2010: Shooters lead India's best-ever medal haul

India won 101 medals, including 38 golds, at New Delhi 2010, making it the country's most successful Commonwealth Games yet. Shooters led the way with 30 medals.

![Image 2: India's Abhinav Bindra and Gagan Narang at Commonwealth Games 2010_GettyImages-104783352](https://img.olympics.com/images/image/private/t_s_16_9_g_auto/t_s_w1460/f_auto/primary/caiq9miepx2vrvqofrr3)

Picture by Getty Images

By Utathya Nag 01 July 2022 12:10 GMT+0 2 min read

The **2010 Commonwealth Games** in New Delhi will always be special in Indian sports history.

It was the first time that India hosted the **[Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/commonwealth-games-first-edition-year-country-host)** and the country's athletes made sure they celebrated the occasion with performances to remember.

**New Delhi 2010** was **[India's best performance at the Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/india-at-commonwealth-games)** to date. India won a total of 101 medals -- including 38 golds, 27 silver and 36 bronze -- to finish second on the **Commonwealth Games 2010 medals table**.

New Delhi 2010 remains the only time India won more than a 100 medals at any edition of **CWG**. The country's second-best haul is 69 medals, including 30 golds, at Manchester 2002.

At the 2010 CWG, Indian men won 64 medals while the women pitched in with 36. The only mixed team medal came in [badminton](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/badminton-guide-how-to-play-rules-olympic-history), a silver.

Australia topped the **2010 Commonwealth Games medals tally** with 177 medals, garnished with 74 golds.

The Indian medal rush was spearheaded by the shooting contingent, headlined by Beijing 2008 Olympic champion [Abhinav Bindra](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/who-abhinav-bindra-indian-shooter-gold-medal-beijing-2008-olympics). [Indian shooters](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/india-shooting-olympic-games-medals) accounted for 30 of India’s 101 medals and 14 of the 38 top podium finishes.

Omkar Singh, Gagan Narang and Vijay Kumar each returned with three golds.

Wrestlers, too, shone with 19 of the 21 Indian grapplers participating at the 2010 CWG stepping on the podium.

Additionally, the 2010 Commonwealth Games also marked many firsts for [Indian athletes](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/famous-indian-athletes-athletics-track-and-field-list). Geeta Phogat created history by becoming the first Indian woman wrestler to win a gold medal at the Commonwealth Games after dominating the women's 55kg category.

Meanwhile, Ashish Kumar registered India's first Commonwealth Games medal in gymnastics after he won a silver and bronze.

Krishna Poonia's discus throw gold at New Delhi 2010 also ended India's 52-year long wait for a top podium finish in an [athletics](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/athletics-track-and-field-sprints-marathons-jumps-throws-heptathlon-decathlon) event at the CWG.

[Milkha Singh](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/milkha-singh-record-commonwealth-gold-asian-games-olympics-indian-athletics)'s win in the men’s 440 yards race at[Cardiff 1958](https://olympics.com/en/news/first-indian-win-gold-medal-commonwealth-games) was India's only athletics gold medal at the Commonwealth Games until then.

A total of 4,352 athletes from 36 different nations and territories competed in the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi. The Indian contingent was 495-member strong.

# Commonwealth Games 2010: Shooters lead India's best-ever medal haul

India won 101 medals, including 38 golds, at New Delhi 2010, making it the country's most successful Commonwealth Games yet. Shooters led the way with 30 medals.

![Image 2: India's Abhinav Bindra and Gagan Narang at Commonwealth Games 2010_GettyImages-104783352](https://img.olympics.com/images/image/private/t_s_16_9_g_auto/t_s_w1460/f_auto/primary/caiq9miepx2vrvqofrr3)

Picture by Getty Images

By Utathya Nag 01 July 2022 12:10 GMT+0 2 min read

The **2010 Commonwealth Games** in New Delhi will always be special in Indian sports history.

It was the first time that India hosted the **[Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/commonwealth-games-first-edition-year-country-host)** and the country's athletes made sure they celebrated the occasion with performances to remember.

**New Delhi 2010** was **[India's best performance at the Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/india-at-commonwealth-games)** to date. India won a total of 101 medals -- including 38 golds, 27 silver and 36 bronze -- to finish second on the **Commonwealth Games 2010 medals table**.

New Delhi 2010 remains the only time India won more than a 100 medals at any edition of **CWG**. The country's second-best haul is 69 medals, including 30 golds, at Manchester 2002.

At the 2010 CWG, Indian men won 64 medals while the women pitched in with 36. The only mixed team medal came in [badminton](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/badminton-guide-how-to-play-rules-olympic-history), a silver.

Australia topped the **2010 Commonwealth Games medals tally** with 177 medals, garnished with 74 golds.

The Indian medal rush was spearheaded by the shooting contingent, headlined by Beijing 2008 Olympic champion [Abhinav Bindra](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/who-abhinav-bindra-indian-shooter-gold-medal-beijing-2008-olympics). [Indian shooters](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/india-shooting-olympic-games-medals) accounted for 30 of India’s 101 medals and 14 of the 38 top podium finishes.

Omkar Singh, Gagan Narang and Vijay Kumar each returned with three golds.

Wrestlers, too, shone with 19 of the 21 Indian grapplers participating at the 2010 CWG stepping on the podium.

Additionally, the 2010 Commonwealth Games also marked many firsts for [Indian athletes](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/famous-indian-athletes-athletics-track-and-field-list). Geeta Phogat created history by becoming the first Indian woman wrestler to win a gold medal at the Commonwealth Games after dominating the women's 55kg category.

Meanwhile, Ashish Kumar registered India's first Commonwealth Games medal in gymnastics after he won a silver and bronze.

Krishna Poonia's discus throw gold at New Delhi 2010 also ended India's 52-year long wait for a top podium finish in an [athletics](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/athletics-track-and-field-sprints-marathons-jumps-throws-heptathlon-decathlon) event at the CWG.

[Milkha Singh](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/milkha-singh-record-commonwealth-gold-asian-games-olympics-indian-athletics)'s win in the men’s 440 yards race at[Cardiff 1958](https://olympics.com/en/news/first-indian-win-gold-medal-commonwealth-games) was India's only athletics gold medal at the Commonwealth Games until then.

A total of 4,352 athletes from 36 different nations and territories competed in the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi. The Indian contingent was 495-member strong.

The 2010 Commonwealth Games (officially known as the XIX [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games "Commonwealth Games")), was a [multi-sport event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-sport_event "Multi-sport event") held in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), India from 3 to 14 October 2010. It was the first time that India hosted the Commonwealth Games and the second time it was held in Asia after [Kuala Lumpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuala_Lumpur "Kuala Lumpur"), Malaysia in [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Commonwealth_Games "1998 Commonwealth Games"). A total of 6,081 athletes from 71 [Commonwealth Games Associations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_Association "Commonwealth Games Association") (CGAs) participated in this Games, competing in 272 events in 21 [sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_sports "Commonwealth Games sports").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-pearson-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-yas-2)

Athletes from 36 participating CGAs won at least one medal; athletes from 23 of these CGAs secured at least one gold. [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Australia at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") led the medal table for the sixth consecutive time with 74 golds and 177 medals overall.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-whitsundaytimes-3) Host nation India finished second in the table for the first time in Commonwealth Games history with a tally of 38 golds and 101 medals overall.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-cwgdelhi2010_news-4)[Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana "Botswana"), the [Cayman Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayman_Islands "Cayman Islands") and [Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoa "Samoa") won their first ever Commonwealth Games gold medals.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-5) Australian swimmer [Alicia Coutts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alicia_Coutts "Alicia Coutts") emerged as the most successful athlete with five gold medals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-6)

Medalists of the [Badminton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badminton_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Badminton at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") mixed team event. From the left: India (silver), [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Malaysia at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") (gold), and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "England at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") (bronze)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/2010_CWG_50_metre_rifle_prone_singles_women.png/250px-2010_CWG_50_metre_rifle_prone_singles_women.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2010_CWG_50_metre_rifle_prone_singles_women.png)

Left to right: [Tejaswini Sawant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tejaswini_Sawant "Tejaswini Sawant") (silver), Jen McIntosh (gold), and Johanne Brekke (bronze) with the medals they earned in [50 metre rifle prone singles women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shooting_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Shooting at the 2010 Commonwealth Games")

The ranking in this table is consistent with [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") convention in its published medal tables. By default, the table is ordered by the number of gold medals the athletes from a nation have won (in this context, a "nation" is an entity represented by an NOC). The number of silver medals is taken into consideration next and then the number of bronze medals. If nations are still tied, equal ranking is given and they are listed alphabetically by IOC country code.

In [Boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Boxing at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") two bronze medals were awarded in each weight class. Additionally there was a tie of three athletes for the third place in the [women's pole vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_pole_vault "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's pole vault") in [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") meant that three bronze medals were awarded. Therefore, the total number of bronze medals is greater than the total number of gold or silver medals.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-cbcnews-7)

## Changes in medal standings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Changes in medal standings")]

### Wrestling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Wrestling")]

#### Men's Greco-Roman – 96 kg

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Men's Greco-Roman – 96 kg")]

Silver medallist [Hassene Fkiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassene_Fkiri "Hassene Fkiri") of Australia was disqualified from the entire competition for making an obscene gesture at the judges. [Kakoma Bella-Lufu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakoma_Bella-Lufu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kakoma Bella-Lufu (page does not exist)") of South Africa was elevated from bronze to silver. [Eric Feunekes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Feunekes?action=edit&redlink=1 "Eric Feunekes (page does not exist)") of Canada was elevated from 4th to the bronze medal position. [[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-9)

### Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Athletics")]

#### Women's 100 metres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Women's 100 metres")]

[Sally Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Pearson "Sally Pearson"), an Australian hurdles specialist, was the initial winner of the gold medal in the [women's 100 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_100_metres "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's 100 metres") contest. However, the English Commonwealth Association launched an appeal arguing that Pearson had also false started at the same time that [Laura Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Turner_(sprinter) "Laura Turner (sprinter)") was disqualified for doing so. A final decision could not be made before the final as the chief start judge had left the stadium and the starter has no authority to disqualify an athlete. Pearson was disqualified later that night but a delay in communication meant Pearson was only told of the decision against her immediately prior to the medal ceremony. Nigeria's [Oludamola Osayomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oludamola_Osayomi "Oludamola Osayomi") was promoted to the gold medal, while [Natasha Mayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natasha_Mayers "Natasha Mayers") of [Saint Vincent and the Grenadines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Vincent_and_the_Grenadines "Saint Vincent and the Grenadines") and English athlete [Katherine Endacott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katherine_Endacott "Katherine Endacott") were elevated to the silver and bronze positions, respectively.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-10) On 11 October [Oludamola Osayomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oludamola_Osayomi "Oludamola Osayomi") was reported to have tested positive for the banned stimulant [Methylhexaneamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylhexaneamine "Methylhexaneamine"). She was disqualified from the gold medal position on 12 October[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-11) and as a result Natasha Mayers and Katherine Endacott was promoted to the gold and silver positions respectively while Bertille Delphine Atangana of Cameroon was promoted to the bronze position.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-12)

#### Women's 400 metres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Women's 400 metres")]

On 15 October it was announced that silver medallist [Folashade Abugan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folashade_Abugan "Folashade Abugan") had been disqualified after testing positive for testosterone prohormone. [Aliann Pompey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliann_Pompey "Aliann Pompey") of [Guyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyana "Guyana") was promoted to the silver medal position, with the bronze medal going to [Christine Amertil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Amertil "Christine Amertil") of the Bahamas.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-bbcsport-13)

#### Women's 4 x 400 metres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Women's 4 x 400 metres")]

Following the positive doping test recorded by [Folashade Abugan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folashade_Abugan "Folashade Abugan") Nigeria were disqualified from second place. England were promoted to the silver medal position, with the bronze medal going to Canada.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-bbcsport-13)

### Boxing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Boxing")]

#### Bantamweight

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Bantamweight")]

On 8 May 2011 Sri Lanka's [Manju Wanniarachchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manju_Wanniarachchi "Manju Wanniarachchi") was provisionally disqualified by the [Commonwealth Games Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_Federation "Commonwealth Games Federation") after testing positive for [Norandrosterone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norandrosterone "Norandrosterone") during the Games. He had 21 days to appeal the decision but on 26 May announced that he did not wish to file an appeal and retired from the sport. On 6 June 2011 the Commonwealth Games Federation announced [Sean McGoldrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_McGoldrick "Sean McGoldrick") of Wales as the new gold medallist. [Tirafalo Seoko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirafalo_Seoko?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tirafalo Seoko (page does not exist)") of Botswana was upgraded from bronze to silver on the basis that he had lost to Wanniarachchi in the semi-finals. [Nicholas Okoth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Okoth "Nicholas Okoth") of Kenya joins [Louis Julie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Julie?action=edit&redlink=1 "Louis Julie (page does not exist)") from Mauritius as a bronze medal winner..[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-morethanthegames-14)

The 2010 Commonwealth Games (officially known as the XIX [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games "Commonwealth Games")), was a [multi-sport event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-sport_event "Multi-sport event") held in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), India from 3 to 14 October 2010. It was the first time that India hosted the Commonwealth Games and the second time it was held in Asia after [Kuala Lumpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuala_Lumpur "Kuala Lumpur"), Malaysia in [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Commonwealth_Games "1998 Commonwealth Games"). A total of 6,081 athletes from 71 [Commonwealth Games Associations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_Association "Commonwealth Games Association") (CGAs) participated in this Games, competing in 272 events in 21 [sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_sports "Commonwealth Games sports").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-pearson-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-yas-2)

Athletes from 36 participating CGAs won at least one medal; athletes from 23 of these CGAs secured at least one gold. [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Australia at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") led the medal table for the sixth consecutive time with 74 golds and 177 medals overall.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-whitsundaytimes-3) Host nation India finished second in the table for the first time in Commonwealth Games history with a tally of 38 golds and 101 medals overall.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-cwgdelhi2010_news-4)[Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana "Botswana"), the [Cayman Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayman_Islands "Cayman Islands") and [Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoa "Samoa") won their first ever Commonwealth Games gold medals.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-5) Australian swimmer [Alicia Coutts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alicia_Coutts "Alicia Coutts") emerged as the most successful athlete with five gold medals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-6)

The ranking in this table is consistent with [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") convention in its published medal tables. By default, the table is ordered by the number of gold medals the athletes from a nation have won (in this context, a "nation" is an entity represented by an NOC). The number of silver medals is taken into consideration next and then the number of bronze medals. If nations are still tied, equal ranking is given and they are listed alphabetically by IOC country code.

In [Boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Boxing at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") two bronze medals were awarded in each weight class. Additionally there was a tie of three athletes for the third place in the [women's pole vault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_pole_vault "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's pole vault") in [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games") meant that three bronze medals were awarded. #### Men's Greco-Roman – 96 kg

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Men's Greco-Roman – 96 kg")]

Silver medallist [Hassene Fkiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassene_Fkiri "Hassene Fkiri") of Australia was disqualified from the entire competition for making an obscene gesture at the judges. [Kakoma Bella-Lufu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakoma_Bella-Lufu?action=edit&redlink=1 "Kakoma Bella-Lufu (page does not exist)") of South Africa was elevated from bronze to silver. ### Athletics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Athletics")]

#### Women's 100 metres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Women's 100 metres")]

[Sally Pearson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Pearson "Sally Pearson"), an Australian hurdles specialist, was the initial winner of the gold medal in the [women's 100 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_100_metres "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's 100 metres") contest. However, the English Commonwealth Association launched an appeal arguing that Pearson had also false started at the same time that [Laura Turner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Turner_(sprinter) "Laura Turner (sprinter)") was disqualified for doing so. A final decision could not be made before the final as the chief start judge had left the stadium and the starter has no authority to disqualify an athlete. Pearson was disqualified later that night but a delay in communication meant Pearson was only told of the decision against her immediately prior to the medal ceremony. Nigeria's [Oludamola Osayomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oludamola_Osayomi "Oludamola Osayomi") was promoted to the gold medal, while [Natasha Mayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natasha_Mayers "Natasha Mayers") of [Saint Vincent and the Grenadines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Vincent_and_the_Grenadines "Saint Vincent and the Grenadines") and English athlete [Katherine Endacott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katherine_Endacott "Katherine Endacott") were elevated to the silver and bronze positions, respectively.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-10) On 11 October [Oludamola Osayomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oludamola_Osayomi "Oludamola Osayomi") was reported to have tested positive for the banned stimulant [Methylhexaneamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methylhexaneamine "Methylhexaneamine"). She was disqualified from the gold medal position on 12 October[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-11) and as a result Natasha Mayers and Katherine Endacott was promoted to the gold and silver positions respectively while Bertille Delphine Atangana of Cameroon was promoted to the bronze position.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-12)

#### Women's 400 metres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Women's 400 metres")]

On 15 October it was announced that silver medallist [Folashade Abugan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folashade_Abugan "Folashade Abugan") had been disqualified after testing positive for testosterone prohormone. [Aliann Pompey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aliann_Pompey "Aliann Pompey") of [Guyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyana "Guyana") was promoted to the silver medal position, with the bronze medal going to [Christine Amertil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Amertil "Christine Amertil") of the Bahamas.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-bbcsport-13)

#### Women's 4 x 400 metres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Women's 4 x 400 metres")]

Following the positive doping test recorded by [Folashade Abugan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folashade_Abugan "Folashade Abugan") Nigeria were disqualified from second place. England were promoted to the silver medal position, with the bronze medal going to Canada.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games_medal_table#cite_note-bbcsport-13)

#### Bantamweight

On 8 May 2011 Sri Lanka's [Manju Wanniarachchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manju_Wanniarachchi "Manju Wanniarachchi") was provisionally disqualified by the [Commonwealth Games Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_Federation "Commonwealth Games Federation") after testing positive for [Norandrosterone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norandrosterone "Norandrosterone") during the Games. He had 21 days to appeal the decision but on 26 May announced that he did not wish to file an appeal and retired from the sport. On 6 June 2011 the Commonwealth Games Federation announced [Sean McGoldrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_McGoldrick "Sean McGoldrick") of Wales as the new gold medallist. [Tirafalo Seoko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirafalo_Seoko?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tirafalo Seoko (page does not exist)") of Botswana was upgraded from bronze to silver on the basis that he had lost to Wanniarachchi in the semi-finals. This map shows list of nations ranked by the medals won by their athletes during XIX Commonwealth Games 2010, held in New Delhi, India, from 3 October to 14 October 2010. The Commonwealth Games is an international, multi-sport event which is held every four years and features competitions involving thousands of elite athletes from members of the [Commonwealth of Nations](http://chartsbin.com/view/ly9 "Commonwealth of Nations").

*   Approximately 6081 athletes from 72 nations are participated in 17 sports.
*   Australia again topped the medal tally for the 6th consecutive time with 74 golds & 177 medals overall.
*   Host nation India emerged as the surprise No. 2 for the very first time in Commonwealth Games history, with a tally of 38 golds & 101 medals overall.
*   Botswana and the Cayman Islands won their first ever Commonwealth games gold medal.

**Note:** The Commonwealth Games Associations are ranked by number of gold medals first, with number of silver then bronze medals acting as the rank decider in the event of equal standing. Other alternative methods of ranking include listing by total medals.

## Delhi 2010

# Delhi 2010 Commonwealth Games

A new look Team England overcame the difficulties of Delhi and finished third in the medals table thanks to gold medals from the likes of Tom Daley and Rebecca Adlington.

Team England won medals in all but one sport with 37 gold, 59 silver and 44 bronze to finish third in the medals table. It was the first time in 16 years the nation had finished outside the top two with hosts India securing second place on the final day of competition. Despite this ranking Team England won more medals than in Melbourne with 142 overall, their third highest ever medals tally at the Commonwealth Games and the biggest by an England team overseas.

There was victory in the archery and squash medals tables thanks to heroics from the likes of archer Danielle Brown, Team England’s first ever Para-sport athlete to compete in able-bodied competition, and Nick Matthew, who had been crowned world number one squash player for the first time three months earlier. Zoe Smith added her name in the record books by becoming the nation’s first female to win a medal in weightlifting.

## Delhi 2010

# Delhi 2010 Commonwealth Games

A new look Team England overcame the difficulties of Delhi and finished third in the medals table thanks to gold medals from the likes of Tom Daley and Rebecca Adlington.

Team England won medals in all but one sport with 37 gold, 59 silver and 44 bronze to finish third in the medals table. It was the first time in 16 years the nation had finished outside the top two with hosts India securing second place on the final day of competition. Despite this ranking Team England won more medals than in Melbourne with 142 overall, their third highest ever medals tally at the Commonwealth Games and the biggest by an England team overseas.

There was victory in the archery and squash medals tables thanks to heroics from the likes of archer Danielle Brown, Team England’s first ever Para-sport athlete to compete in able-bodied competition, and Nick Matthew, who had been crowned world number one squash player for the first time three months earlier. Zoe Smith added her name in the record books by becoming the nation’s first female to win a medal in weightlifting.

History of the Commonwealth Games

A sporting [competition](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Competition)bringing together the members of the [British Empire](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire)was first proposed by the Reverend Astley Cooper in 1891 when he wrote an article in 

[The Times](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times)

suggesting a "Pan-Britannic-Pan-Anglican Contest and Festival every four years as a means of increasing the goodwill and good understanding of the British Empire". The

Commonwealth Games

is an international, [multi-sport event](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-sport_event)involving athletes from the [Commonwealth of Nations](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations).As well as many [Olympic sports](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sport), the Games also include some sports that are played mainly in Commonwealth countries, such as [lawn bowls](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_bowls), [rugby sevens](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_sevens)and [netball](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netball).

[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-0)

The Games are overseen by the [Commonwealth Games Federation](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_Federation)(CGF), which also controls the sporting programme and selects the host cities. The host city is selected from across the Commonwealth, with eighteen cities in seven countries having hosted it.The event was first held in 1930 under the title of the 

British Empire Games

in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada. The event was renamed as the

British Empire and Commonwealth Games

in 1954, the 

British Commonwealth Games

in 1970, and gained its current title in 1978. Only six teams have attended every Commonwealth Games: [Australia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia), [Canada](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada), [England](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England), [New Zealand](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand), [Scotland](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland)and [Wales](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales). [Australia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia)has been the highest achieving team for ten games, [England](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England)for seven and [Canada](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)for one.In 1911, the [Festival of the Empire](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_the_Empire)was held in come London to celebrate the [coronation](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation)of King [George V](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_V_of_the_United_Kingdom). As part of the festival an Inter-Empire Championships was held in which teams from Australia, Canada, South Africa and the United Kingdom competed in events such as boxing, wrestling, swimming and athletics.In 1928, [Melville Marks Robinson](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melville_Marks_Robinson)of Canada was asked to organise the first ever [British](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire_Games)[Empire Games](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire_Games). These were held in [Hamilton, Canada](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Canada)

two years later.The first Games were held in 1930 in [Hamilton, Ontario](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Ontario), Canada. The name changed to 

British Empire and Commonwealth Games

in 1954, to 

British Commonwealth Games

in 1970 and assumed the current name of the Commonwealth Games in 1978.

History of the Commonwealth Games

A sporting [competition](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Competition)bringing together the members of the [British Empire](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire)was first proposed by the Reverend Astley Cooper in 1891 when he wrote an article in 

[The Times](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times)

suggesting a "Pan-Britannic-Pan-Anglican Contest and Festival every four years as a means of increasing the goodwill and good understanding of the British Empire". The

Commonwealth Games

is an international, [multi-sport event](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-sport_event)involving athletes from the [Commonwealth of Nations](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations).As well as many [Olympic sports](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_sport), the Games also include some sports that are played mainly in Commonwealth countries, such as [lawn bowls](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_bowls), [rugby sevens](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_sevens)and [netball](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netball).

[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-0)

The Games are overseen by the [Commonwealth Games Federation](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games_Federation)(CGF), which also controls the sporting programme and selects the host cities. The host city is selected from across the Commonwealth, with eighteen cities in seven countries having hosted it.The event was first held in 1930 under the title of the 

British Empire Games

in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada. The event was renamed as the

British Empire and Commonwealth Games

in 1954, the 

British Commonwealth Games

in 1970, and gained its current title in 1978. Only six teams have attended every Commonwealth Games: [Australia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia), [Canada](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada), [England](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England), [New Zealand](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand), [Scotland](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland)and [Wales](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales). [Australia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia)has been the highest achieving team for ten games, [England](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England)for seven and [Canada](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada)for one.In 1911, the [Festival of the Empire](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_the_Empire)was held in come London to celebrate the [coronation](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation)of King [George V](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_V_of_the_United_Kingdom). As part of the festival an Inter-Empire Championships was held in which teams from Australia, Canada, South Africa and the United Kingdom competed in events such as boxing, wrestling, swimming and athletics.In 1928, [Melville Marks Robinson](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melville_Marks_Robinson)of Canada was asked to organise the first ever [British](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire_Games)[Empire Games](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire_Games). These were held in [Hamilton, Canada](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Canada)

two years later.The first Games were held in 1930 in [Hamilton, Ontario](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_Ontario), Canada. The name changed to 

British Empire and Commonwealth Games

in 1954, to 

British Commonwealth Games

in 1970 and assumed the current name of the Commonwealth Games in 1978.

[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-Story-1)

The correct answer is **101**.

![Image 3](https://cdn.testbook.com/resources/lms_creative_elements/key-point-image.png)Key Points

*   India achieved its highest-ever medal tally of **101 medals** at the **2010 Commonwealth Games** held in Delhi, India.
*   This tally included **39 gold, 26 silver, and 36 bronze medals**, showcasing India's best performance in the history of the Commonwealth Games.
*   The 2010 Commonwealth Games was the **19th edition** of the event and marked the first time India hosted the games.
*   India ranked **second** in the medal tally, with Australia finishing first and England in third place.
*   Sports such as wrestling, shooting, and athletics were key contributors to India's success in the 2010 edition.

![Image 4](https://cdn.testbook.com/resources/lms_creative_elements/additional-information-image.png)**Additional Information**

*   **Commonwealth Games Overview:**
    *   The Commonwealth Games is a multi-sport event held every four years involving athletes from the Commonwealth of Nations.
    *   It was first held in 1930 as the British Empire Games in Hamilton, Canada.
    *   India has been participating in the Commonwealth Games since 1934 and has consistently improved its performance over the years.

*   **Highlights of the 2010 Commonwealth Games:**
    *   Wrestler Sushil Kumar, shooter Gagan Narang, and boxer Vijender Singh were among the standout performers for India.
    *   India's performance in shooting and wrestling played a significant role in achieving the record-breaking medal tally.
    *   The event witnessed participation from 71 nations and territories.

*   **India's Best Performances in Commonwealth Games:**
    *   India's second-best performance occurred during the 2018 Gold Coast Commonwealth Games, where the country secured 66 medals.
    *   India has consistently performed well in sports like shooting, wrestling, weightlifting, and badminton.

*   **Significance of the 2010 Commonwealth Games:**
    *   The 2010 Games helped India establish itself as a major sporting nation in the Commonwealth.
    *   It also highlighted India's organizational capabilities, despite challenges in preparation and controversies.

![Image 3](https://cdn.testbook.com/resources/lms_creative_elements/key-point-image.png)Key Points

*   India achieved its highest-ever medal tally of **101 medals** at the **2010 Commonwealth Games** held in Delhi, India.
*   This tally included **39 gold, 26 silver, and 36 bronze medals**, showcasing India's best performance in the history of the Commonwealth Games.
*   The 2010 Commonwealth Games was the **19th edition** of the event and marked the first time India hosted the games.
*   India ranked **second** in the medal tally, with Australia finishing first and England in third place.
*   Sports such as wrestling, shooting, and athletics were key contributors to India's success in the 2010 edition.

![Image 4](https://cdn.testbook.com/resources/lms_creative_elements/additional-information-image.png)**Additional Information**

*   **Commonwealth Games Overview:**
    *   The Commonwealth Games is a multi-sport event held every four years involving athletes from the Commonwealth of Nations.
    *   It was first held in 1930 as the British Empire Games in Hamilton, Canada.
    *   India has been participating in the Commonwealth Games since 1934 and has consistently improved its performance over the years.

*   **Highlights of the 2010 Commonwealth Games:**
    *   Wrestler Sushil Kumar, shooter Gagan Narang, and boxer Vijender Singh were among the standout performers for India.
    *   India's performance in shooting and wrestling played a significant role in achieving the record-breaking medal tally.
    *   The event witnessed participation from 71 nations and territories.

*   **India's Best Performances in Commonwealth Games:**
    *   India's second-best performance occurred during the 2018 Gold Coast Commonwealth Games, where the country secured 66 medals.
    *   India has consistently performed well in sports like shooting, wrestling, weightlifting, and badminton.

*   **Significance of the 2010 Commonwealth Games:**
    *   The 2010 Games helped India establish itself as a major sporting nation in the Commonwealth.
    *   It also highlighted India's organizational capabilities, despite challenges in preparation and controversies.

[India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") hosted the 2010 Commonwealth Games which were held in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi") from 3 to 14 October 2010. India won 101 medals in total, including 38 Gold medals, enabling it to finish the Games at second position behind [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"). For the first time in the history of the Games India won over 100 medals in total. For the first time in the history of the Games, India won a medal in [Gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics "Gymnastics"), where [Ashish Kumar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashish_Kumar_(gymnast) "Ashish Kumar (gymnast)") won a Silver and a Bronze. And it was after a gap of 52 years that India won a Gold in Athletics when [Krishna Poonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krishna_Poonia "Krishna Poonia") won Gold in [Women's discus throw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_discus_throw "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's discus throw") and when [Geeta Phogat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geeta_Phogat "Geeta Phogat") won India's first ever gold medal in women's wrestling.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-2)

[India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") hosted the 2010 Commonwealth Games which were held in [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi") from 3 to 14 October 2010. India won 101 medals in total, including 38 Gold medals, enabling it to finish the Games at second position behind [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"). For the first time in the history of the Games India won over 100 medals in total. For the first time in the history of the Games, India won a medal in [Gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics "Gymnastics"), where [Ashish Kumar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashish_Kumar_(gymnast) "Ashish Kumar (gymnast)") won a Silver and a Bronze. And it was after a gap of 52 years that India won a Gold in Athletics when [Krishna Poonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krishna_Poonia "Krishna Poonia") won Gold in [Women's discus throw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games_%E2%80%93_Women's_discus_throw "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games – Women's discus throw") and when [Geeta Phogat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geeta_Phogat "Geeta Phogat") won India's first ever gold medal in women's wrestling.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games#cite_note-2)

# Commonwealth Games 2010: Shooters lead India's best-ever medal haul

India won 101 medals, including 38 golds, at New Delhi 2010, making it the country's most successful Commonwealth Games yet. Shooters led the way with 30 medals.

![Image 2: India's Abhinav Bindra and Gagan Narang at Commonwealth Games 2010_GettyImages-104783352](https://img.olympics.com/images/image/private/t_s_16_9_g_auto/t_s_w1460/f_auto/primary/caiq9miepx2vrvqofrr3)

Picture by Getty Images

By Utathya Nag 01 July 2022 12:10 GMT+0 2 min read

The **2010 Commonwealth Games** in New Delhi will always be special in Indian sports history.

It was the first time that India hosted the **[Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/commonwealth-games-first-edition-year-country-host)** and the country's athletes made sure they celebrated the occasion with performances to remember.

**New Delhi 2010** was **[India's best performance at the Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/india-at-commonwealth-games)** to date. India won a total of 101 medals -- including 38 golds, 27 silver and 36 bronze -- to finish second on the **Commonwealth Games 2010 medals table**.

New Delhi 2010 remains the only time India won more than a 100 medals at any edition of **CWG**. The country's second-best haul is 69 medals, including 30 golds, at Manchester 2002.

At the 2010 CWG, Indian men won 64 medals while the women pitched in with 36. The only mixed team medal came in [badminton](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/badminton-guide-how-to-play-rules-olympic-history), a silver.

Australia topped the **2010 Commonwealth Games medals tally** with 177 medals, garnished with 74 golds.

The Indian medal rush was spearheaded by the shooting contingent, headlined by Beijing 2008 Olympic champion [Abhinav Bindra](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/who-abhinav-bindra-indian-shooter-gold-medal-beijing-2008-olympics). [Indian shooters](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/india-shooting-olympic-games-medals) accounted for 30 of India’s 101 medals and 14 of the 38 top podium finishes.

Omkar Singh, Gagan Narang and Vijay Kumar each returned with three golds.

Wrestlers, too, shone with 19 of the 21 Indian grapplers participating at the 2010 CWG stepping on the podium.

Additionally, the 2010 Commonwealth Games also marked many firsts for [Indian athletes](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/famous-indian-athletes-athletics-track-and-field-list). Geeta Phogat created history by becoming the first Indian woman wrestler to win a gold medal at the Commonwealth Games after dominating the women's 55kg category.

Meanwhile, Ashish Kumar registered India's first Commonwealth Games medal in gymnastics after he won a silver and bronze.

Krishna Poonia's discus throw gold at New Delhi 2010 also ended India's 52-year long wait for a top podium finish in an [athletics](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/athletics-track-and-field-sprints-marathons-jumps-throws-heptathlon-decathlon) event at the CWG.

[Milkha Singh](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/milkha-singh-record-commonwealth-gold-asian-games-olympics-indian-athletics)'s win in the men’s 440 yards race at[Cardiff 1958](https://olympics.com/en/news/first-indian-win-gold-medal-commonwealth-games) was India's only athletics gold medal at the Commonwealth Games until then.

A total of 4,352 athletes from 36 different nations and territories competed in the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi. The Indian contingent was 495-member strong.

# Commonwealth Games 2010: Shooters lead India's best-ever medal haul

India won 101 medals, including 38 golds, at New Delhi 2010, making it the country's most successful Commonwealth Games yet. Shooters led the way with 30 medals.

![Image 2: India's Abhinav Bindra and Gagan Narang at Commonwealth Games 2010_GettyImages-104783352](https://img.olympics.com/images/image/private/t_s_16_9_g_auto/t_s_w1460/f_auto/primary/caiq9miepx2vrvqofrr3)

Picture by Getty Images

By Utathya Nag 01 July 2022 12:10 GMT+0 2 min read

The **2010 Commonwealth Games** in New Delhi will always be special in Indian sports history.

It was the first time that India hosted the **[Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/commonwealth-games-first-edition-year-country-host)** and the country's athletes made sure they celebrated the occasion with performances to remember.

**New Delhi 2010** was **[India's best performance at the Commonwealth Games](https://olympics.com/en/news/india-at-commonwealth-games)** to date. India won a total of 101 medals -- including 38 golds, 27 silver and 36 bronze -- to finish second on the **Commonwealth Games 2010 medals table**.

New Delhi 2010 remains the only time India won more than a 100 medals at any edition of **CWG**. The country's second-best haul is 69 medals, including 30 golds, at Manchester 2002.

At the 2010 CWG, Indian men won 64 medals while the women pitched in with 36. The only mixed team medal came in [badminton](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/badminton-guide-how-to-play-rules-olympic-history), a silver.

Australia topped the **2010 Commonwealth Games medals tally** with 177 medals, garnished with 74 golds.

The Indian medal rush was spearheaded by the shooting contingent, headlined by Beijing 2008 Olympic champion [Abhinav Bindra](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/who-abhinav-bindra-indian-shooter-gold-medal-beijing-2008-olympics). [Indian shooters](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/india-shooting-olympic-games-medals) accounted for 30 of India’s 101 medals and 14 of the 38 top podium finishes.

Omkar Singh, Gagan Narang and Vijay Kumar each returned with three golds.

Wrestlers, too, shone with 19 of the 21 Indian grapplers participating at the 2010 CWG stepping on the podium.

Additionally, the 2010 Commonwealth Games also marked many firsts for [Indian athletes](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/famous-indian-athletes-athletics-track-and-field-list). Geeta Phogat created history by becoming the first Indian woman wrestler to win a gold medal at the Commonwealth Games after dominating the women's 55kg category.

Meanwhile, Ashish Kumar registered India's first Commonwealth Games medal in gymnastics after he won a silver and bronze.

Krishna Poonia's discus throw gold at New Delhi 2010 also ended India's 52-year long wait for a top podium finish in an [athletics](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/athletics-track-and-field-sprints-marathons-jumps-throws-heptathlon-decathlon) event at the CWG.

[Milkha Singh](https://www.olympics.com/en/news/milkha-singh-record-commonwealth-gold-asian-games-olympics-indian-athletics)'s win in the men’s 440 yards race at[Cardiff 1958](https://olympics.com/en/news/first-indian-win-gold-medal-commonwealth-games) was India's only athletics gold medal at the Commonwealth Games until then.

A total of 4,352 athletes from 36 different nations and territories competed in the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi. The Indian contingent was 495-member strong.
